The extract chosen from Act 3 is a pivotal moment in the play, and the majority of candidates were able to place it successfully and understand its significance, with many seeing the appearance of Banquo’s ghost as a manifestation of Macbeth’s guilt. A small minority were under the impression that this was the ghost of Duncan, despite the opening stage direction but, overall, examiners felt that it was an extremely accessible extract with plenty of material to for candidates to explore.

Better responses were able to see the various levels of dramatic irony in the scene, beginning with Macbeth’s duplicitous comments on Banquo’s absence from the feast and their effect on an audience. Many looked at the polite, respectful language of the thanes towards their new king, before focusing on the sudden change in mood when Macbeth sees the ghost of Banquo. There were thoughtful comments from some on the significance of the ghost sitting “in Macbeth’s place” and most candidates were able to achieve good coverage, with lots of attention given to Lady Macbeth’s intervention in the latter part of the extract. While many only saw this as further evidence of her controlling nature, stronger responses had a more nuanced understanding that recognised her embarrassment and desire to protect their newly acquired power. Most candidates saw Lady Macbeth’s comments at the end of the extract as a continuation of her manipulation and emasculation of her husband in Acts 1 and 2, though more assured responses were able to note Macbeth’s assertive response “Ay and a bold one” and could see this as evidence of her power diminishing in their relationship.

13 Weaker responses tended to misunderstand the opening of the extract, believing that Macbeth sees the ghost immediately, or struggling to say much about his interaction with the thanes. While most looked at Macbeth’s reaction to the ghost with “never shake / Thy gory locks at me,” the most scrutinized line, examiners noted that some seemed reluctant to dig further into language choices. Some pounced on Macbeth’s use of the word “devil,” though rarely with a clear idea of why he uses it. Lady Macbeth’s significant intervention prompted plenty of discussion, though some missed the stage direction “to Macbeth” and therefore didn’t realise that the Thanes and Macbeth were addressed separately, with a marked change in tone. Predictably, much was made of “Are you a man?,” although for some it led into a contextual cul-de-sac, and opportunities to explore the final speech, with its exasperated tone and imagery, were not taken as a result. The clear message from examiners is that candidates must resist the temptation to discourse on James I’s obsession with the supernatural and expectations of Jacobean women and instead explore the events, ideas, and language of the extract.
c720u10-jun24-22-q:
Examiners felt that this was an extremely open and accessible question, which allowed for a variety of different approaches. Most candidates opted to look at a single character, tracking them across the play and looking at where they might gain or lose sympathy. Others looked at several characters before deciding which of them most deserves sympathy. While the majority answered on Macbeth or Lady Macbeth, examiners saw some excellent responses on Macduff, with Banquo and Duncan also featuring, although candidates that wrote exclusively on one of the latter two were often self-limiting, due to these characters’ deaths in Act 2 and Act 3, respectively. Examiners reported that the question encouraged candidates to use their evaluative skills, and some noted that responses sometimes included considered, personal justifications.

Weaker students tended to not cover the whole play, sometimes confining their responses to the first half of the play. A lack of textual references inhibited marks, and there were a few narrative responses on the main characters that neglected a clear focus on sympathy or offered little textual support, or both. Higher level responses were able to cover the whole text, sometimes comparing specific details across scenes to show changes in the selected character(s), as well as providing opportunities for language analysis. Such responses also tended to be evaluative, appreciating the complex nature of their character(s) and making nuanced judgements on sympathy.

In last year’s report, examiners raised the issue of Lady Macbeth receiving a disproportionate amount of criticism, whether due to inaccurate readings or misogyny. This year there were many responses that argued for sympathy for Macbeth that blamed almost everything on his wife, conveniently ignoring details such as his thoughts of murdering Duncan as soon as he is made Thane of Cawdor and his “black and deep desires” when Malcolm is named Prince of Cumberland – not to mention her lack of involvement in any of Macbeth’s murders after the killing of Duncan. Interestingly, some candidates took the opportunity to argue for sympathy for Lady Macbeth, some very successfully. However, candidates sometimes based their argument on Lady Macbeth losing a baby before the start of the play or got involved in extended contextual discussion of the restrictions on women in Jacobean times. Both tended to lead to underachievement. To re-iterate: more balance and nuance in discussion of Lady Macbeth would be beneficial, but it must be rooted in the play’s events and language.
c720u10-jun24-31-q:
Most candidates recognised this extract from Act 1 Scene 2 and were aware that it gives the audience an early view of Othello’s character while under pressure from an angry Brabantio. Othello was seen as a calm, eloquent peacemaker in the face of Brabantio’s vitriolic, racist accusations. Most candidates were able to explore Brabantio’s racism and claims of Othello’s use of black magic, with popular quotations including “foul thief,” “stowed my daughter,” “chains of magic” and “sooty bosom.” Many focused on possible audience responses to his discriminatory language and the objectification of Desdemona.

Stronger responses tracked through the whole extract, commenting on the presentation of characters, and picking up on the clear contrasts between them, often exploring this through AO2 analysis. There was a sense of the significance of the extract, and some saw foreshadowing of later events. Examiners noted that understanding of Brabantio here was often quite perceptive, with higher level responses seeing his mounting frustration at his lack of agency when faced with Othello’s polite, quietly commanding presence.

Weaker responses tended not to look at the latter part of the extract, and some barely considered Othello’s part in the exchange at all, instead looking exclusively at Brabantio’s main speech. Othello’s “Were it my cue to fight…” was frequently misunderstood, and some candidates lost focus either by moving beyond the extract into later events or getting bogged down in contextual comments, usually on the treatment of women in Shakespeare’s time. As with other extract questions, a reluctance to address AO2 was the most limiting factor here.
c720u10-jun24-32-q:
Examiners felt that candidates wrote well on Iago and were able to recall a range of quotations and key events. Some tracked through the play, identifying moments of deception, whereas others discussed different characters in turn. Roderigo was a popular starting point, with candidates exploring his gullibility and Iago’s clever manipulation of him for money and use in his wider machinations. Othello was widely discussed, as expected and, for many, it was at this point that their essays really warmed up. Emilia and Cassio were also discussed, with last year’s extract clearly helping with the latter. Popular moments included the opening scenes, the fight scene, the handkerchief scenes, the manipulation of Cassio and Desdemona’s “affair”, Iago’s soliloquies and the ending. AO2 was often confidently handled, for example how Iago manipulates Othello’s downfall and the contrast in his language towards Desdemona at different points of the play. The use of soliloquy and importance of dramatic irony were widely discussed. Some candidates felt that Iago was deceiving himself, which was an interesting line of analysis. Many candidates discussed Iago’s final line and the lack of knowledge the audience has of his true motivations, with some exploring possible reasons for his actions.

Better responses tended to be sustained, secure discussions of Iago’s deception of others ranging across the play, and examiners noted that many candidates seemed fully invested in exploring his behaviour and motives. They made good use of key quotations, with clear awareness of the importance of probing language choices within them to address AO2. Weaker responses were often brief or simple and lacking in textual support, sometimes confusing characters (for example mixing up Cassio and Roderigo) or being unclear on the sequence of the play’s events.
c720u10-jun24-41-q:
Examiners felt that the extract was handled well, with candidates across the ability range appreciating its significance in the play and maintaining a clear focus on an audience response. A range of viewpoints on Claudio and Benedick were expressed, with the former seen as love-struck, innocent, and polite by more sympathetic candidates, or superficial, naïve, needy, and misogynistic by others. Similarly, Benedick was viewed as either witty, honest, and grounded, or cynical, annoying, and judgmental (particularly about women). The most popular quotations focused on views of Hero, particularly “modest young lady,” “Can the world buy such a jewel?” and “In mine eye, she is the sweetest lady that ever I looked on,” which all provided ample opportunity for AO2 analysis. However, Benedick’s “she was unhandsome” was often viewed outside the complex sentence it sits within and was therefore frequently misunderstood.

14 Stronger responses worked through the whole extract, paying attention to language choices, and addressing structure through appreciation of the use of questions, changes in tone and foreshadowing, with Benedick’s comment on how Hero’s cousin “exceeds her… in beauty” noted as a clear hint to what is to come. Examiners were pleased to see how many candidates had a good appreciation of the humour in the extract, and some higher-level responses did well with some of Benedick’s more outlandish and obscure imagery.

Less successful responses generally struggled to cover the latter half of the extract, or perhaps didn’t take the opportunities to engage with the language and imagery used by the characters beyond “such a jewel”: examiners mentioned that a significant number of candidates showed reasonable understanding but were nevertheless limited by a lack of attention to AO2. Inevitably, for some, the views on Hero expressed by the characters led to extended comments on the position of women in Elizabethan England that didn’t add much to marks.
c720u10-jun24-42-q:
Ever popular characters, Beatrice and Benedick were written about with confidence by most candidates and at all levels. There was attention to the changes in their relationship and the complexity of their bond, often in comparison with Hero and Claudio. The most popular moments selected for discussion were the opening scenes where their dynamic is established, the masked ball, the gulling scenes, the aftermath of the first wedding and the ending. In particular, examiners felt that candidates wrote well about the gulling and the mirrored reactions of the characters. AO2 was explored through structure by many through tracking character development and identifying the different turning points for the couple. Frequently selected quotations included “merry war”, Signior Mountanto”, “I would rather hear my dog bark at a crow…”, “She speaks poniards and every word stabs”, “I do love nothing in the world so much as you” and “Kill Claudio”.

Better responses were selective and were able to explore language, structure and form at key moments. Some were able to show evaluative skills by contrasting Beatrice and Benedick’s relationship with that of Claudio and Hero. The ability to track the couple right across the play, selecting judiciously, led to high marks, particularly with some comments on the ending and whether Benedick’s “Peace! I will stop your mouth” might signal a change in Beatrice’s behaviour once married. Weaker responses tended to be brief or struggled to cover the whole play. Those who couldn’t bring specific textual references into their responses didn’t get beyond Band 2, while those who wandered into generalised contextual discussion tended to miss greater opportunities for reward in AO1 and AO2.

This extract, from early in the play, seemed familiar to most candidates, and many saw its importance in setting up the audience’s view of Henry before we see him on stage, particularly given his recent “reformation.” However, some candidates would clearly have preferred it to have been taken from elsewhere in Act 1, with Canterbury and Ely’s earlier discussion of the possible loss of “half of (their) possession” to the crown or their subsequent attempt to persuade Henry to lay claim to France making frequent intrusions into answers. Nonetheless, most candidates were able to discuss the bishops’ views of Henry’s impressive start to his reign, with some able to infer their self-interest and condescending attitudes towards Henry’s “unlettered, rude and shallow” former associates. Popular quotations included “Never came reformation in a flood,” “we are blessed in the change” and “The strawberry grows underneath the nettle,” the latter metaphor often enabling candidates to get an instant foothold in the AO2 column of the mark scheme.

Less successful responses misunderstood Canterbury’s criticism of Henry’s past actions as being current misgivings, often leading candidates into a false juxtaposition of Canterbury as a negative voice and Ely as a positive one. A few responses frustrated examiners with their brevity, sometimes only making a couple of textual selections. Better responses were able to track through the extract, showing sound appreciation of the bishops’ delight at Henry’s kingly qualities and probing language choices, for example biblical and religious imagery, Canterbury’s contrasting of Henry’s past and present and Ely’s use of natural imagery.

Merchant of Venice The extract enabled candidates of all abilities to respond: a key set-piece moment from the play, it has a clear narrative and plenty of imagery with which to engage. Most candidates could place this scene within the play and understood the significance of the casket test. Morocco was viewed quite negatively by many candidates, who interpreted his behaviour as bombastic, judgemental, greedy and materialistic; others were more sympathetic, given his disappointment at his incorrect choice of casket and Portia’s attitude towards him. Candidates were empathetic to the position of Portia but disapproved of her racist attitude shown clearly at the end of the extract. Her matter-of-fact response to Morocco’s opening speech, “There take it, prince, and if my form lie there / Then I am yours” was interpreted in a variety of ways, with some believing that she is pushing him towards an incorrect choice and others seeing it as a clear expression of her cold disdain for him (and indeed the casket test itself). Popular textual selections included “ten times undervalued”, “angel in a golden bed”, “all that glisters…” and “all of his complexion”. There were few misunderstandings, although some candidates mistook the writing in the scroll read aloud by Morocco for his own words.

15 Weaker responses tended to lose focus, with some keen to revisit Portia’s earlier comments on Morocco in Act 1 Scene 2 or instead move ahead to Bassanio’s turn at the test, and others drifting into generalised discussion of gender roles or religion in Elizabethan society. While it’s difficult to avoid contextual factors in this play, it’s vital to stay focused on the events depicted and language used within the extract as far as possible. Stronger answers managed to maintain sharp focus on A02, exploring fruitful areas such as the descriptions of the caskets, Morocco’s objectification of Portia and the contrast between Morocco’s two speeches. Attention to Morocco’s frequent use of rhetorical questions, exclamations and use of imagery related to religion and wealth paid off for many, but it was unusual to see candidates address aspects of form such as the pivotal split iambic line as the casket is unlocked, or the use of rhyming couplets in the latter half of the extract.

Characteristics of good extract responses:

• Clear and sustained focus on the question asked and on the details in the extract. • Selection of short, apt references to support points made. • Critical probing of inferences, implicit meanings and subtext as well as more surface ideas. • Wide-ranging coverage of the extract. • Close examination of how the language/imagery used helps to convey meaning.

Ways in which performance could be improved:

• More detailed coverage of the extract, managing comment on the beginning, middle and end, not straying beyond it. • More selection of supporting references rather than general impressions. • Less reference to contextual factors when AO3 is not addressed in this question. • More practice on probing figurative language, connotations and key words to accumulate AO2 marks. • Practice in responding to both soliloquies and extracts with characters interacting and responding to each other.

Examiners felt that the focus on the main characters, relationships and themes in the essay questions enabled candidates of all abilities to show their knowledge and understanding of the play they had studied, and many were impressed with how well-prepared candidates were. Always open to a range of approaches, examiners reported that the relatively open nature of questions such as 12 and 22 provided wide scope for candidates to demonstrate their knowledge, skill, and ideas.

Successful answers tended to either utilise brief plans, or track a character, relationship, or theme across the text chronologically, selecting key moments, as a means of structuring their response. They made good use of textual quotations to support discussion and then probed details for connotations and explored imagery to gain AO2 credit. …

Examiners felt that this question on a controversial figure in the play afforded plenty of scope for candidates to engage and respond. Most showed secure knowledge of Antonio, tracking him across the play, starting with the opening scene. Some, however, took a more selective approach and looked at key moments in non-chronological order to support their view of him. More positive readings of Antonio focused on his love for and loyalty towards Bassanio, sometimes including discussion of the possible homosexual relationship between them, the views of his many friends, his wealth and success, his sadness and his loneliness at the end of the play. Focus on his negative traits included his antisemitism, the hypocrisy of how he treats Shylock, his inability to change or develop, and his lack of remorse over his treatment of Shylock, underlined by his behaviour towards him at the end of the trial. Better answers drew out the two sides to Antonio and the contradictions in his character, often leading to thoughtful evaluation of his varied behaviour in the play. AO2 was covered through language, with effective use of key quotations, and structure (for example, his importance in driving the plot and his opening of the play, the symbolism and significance of the bond, and the cyclical structure of his sadness at both the beginning and the end of the play). Weaker responses tended to be brief or narrative driven, often lacking in specific textual detail and paying only cursory attention to AO2. Contextual reference is often necessary in this play, but those who allow it to dominate discussion tend to lose out by wasting time that would be better spent accumulating AO1 and AO2 marks.

Characteristics of good essay responses: • Close tracking of a character / relationship / theme across the whole text. • Selection of a range of apt events and specific details to support thoughtful ideas. • Some analysis of the writer’s intentions when creating characters and plots. • Highlighting of important turning points and key contrasts and their effects. • Careful spelling and punctuation, with vocabulary and sentence structure used to control meaning effectively.

Ways in which performance could be improved: • Tracking a character / relationship / theme across the whole text, with effective coverage of the play. • More focus on including short quotations that can be analysed for AO2, fewer contextual comments.

20 • Practice in creating clear, cohesive arguments which address the question posed. • Practice in selecting detailed textual evidence for ideas. • Practice in proof-reading responses to avoid technical errors, such as forgetting use of capital letters for character names, neglecting punctuation, abbreviating character names.
c720u10-jun24-71-q:
Last year there were concerns that a significant minority of candidates seemed to treat 71 as if it were an unseen text, and some candidates were not attempting 72. This year, examiners were pleased to report that there was a marked improvement in engagement with the Anthology poetry questions, with exam technique seemingly stronger. Context was addressed with greater confidence, particularly in 71; however, there does still appear to be an issue with knowledge being demonstrated on the chosen poem – in this case Armitage’s “The Manhunt” – not being replicated across both questions.

Both the chosen poem “The Manhunt” and the theme of relationships were accessible for the whole ability range, and examiners got the sense that it was a popular choice that candidates enjoyed writing about. Some, however, chose to ignore the focus on relationships, instead discussing the presentation of war, and missed out on AO1 marks as a result. Many of the poems in the Anthology have several themes, and it is essential for candidates to focus on the one specified in the question to achieve success in these questions. Most candidates, though, were able to track through the poem, selecting and probing key metaphors and phrases, commenting on how the relationship is presented and grasping some key ideas. For 72, a wide range of poems were selected, with popular choices including “A Wife in London”, “Sonnet 43”, “Valentine” and “Cozy Apologia”. “Afternoons” was a choice that tended to work well, and there were some perhaps less obvious selections that proved effective, with Heaney’s relationship with nature explored in “Death of a Naturalist” and the soldiers’ relationship with the earth discussed in “Mametz Wood.” Context was addressed more frequently than last year, though often less securely on the comparison poem than “The Manhunt.”

71 Examiners reported that “The Manhunt” seemed like an extremely popular choice of poem and candidates across the ability range were able to write about the presentation of the relationship, showing understanding and, at the highest levels, sensitivity. Candidates seemed generally well-prepared, and many tackled the question with genuine enthusiasm, tracking through the poem and selecting from the array of metaphors and key phrases on offer: Armitage’s language enabled higher ability candidates to show their analytical skill by unpicking images and probing connotations, while those working in the lower bands were able to show clear awareness of the main ideas in the poem and could discuss Laura Beddoes’ slow exploration of her husband Eddie’s physical and mental health following his return from war – with many naming the characters as a matter of course and therefore gaining AO3 credit.

There were, of course, a few misunderstandings, with the opening couplet often assumed to have taken place pre-war, rather than recognising the “passionate nights and intimate days” as a physical connection immediately after Eddie’s return which pre-empted the emotional reconnection. Some candidates confused Armitage with Eddie, thereby missing out on some contextual knowledge, and a small minority were under the misapprehension that Eddie died, which tended to limit AO1 marks. However, overall, examiners were impressed with candidates’ understanding of the poem.

21 Popular quotations included “passionate nights and intimate days”, “only then”, “the frozen river that ran through his face”, “handle and hold”, “grazed heart”, “foetus of metal” and “a sweating, unexploded mine / Buried deep in his mind”, which provided an array of opportunities to address AO2. Examiners were pleased to report that structure tended to be discussed more successfully than in previous years, whether this was on the rhyme scheme, the “ladder”- like stanzas, the use of enjambement or the journey of the bullet and movement from physical to mental injuries.

Context was generally handled better than in previous years, perhaps due to the Channel 4 documentary for which the poem was originally written, although there was still some confusion with the war in which Eddie served, mainly due to the mixing up of contexts of another war-related poems in the anthology. Examiners noted that contextual information tended to be “front-loaded” in introductions, and candidates tended to do better when it was interleaved throughout the response and linked to particular parts of the poem (for example linking the “unexploded mine” to Eddie’s PTSD). Perhaps more could have been made of the fact that Eddie was a UN Peacekeeper, and therefore often unable to intervene in a war that was characterised by its appalling brutality towards civilians, particularly women and children.

Weaker responses tended to not get all the way through the poem, or not engage with the language, despite the many opportunities the poem offered. Some candidates tracked the surface of the images used to describe Eddie’s damaged body without probing connotations or looking for metaphorical meaning, while others neglected or confused contextual details. Stronger answers were usually characterised by careful tracking through the poem and exploring the sub-text of Armitage’s imagery with a clear focus on Laura’s gentle but determined search for the source of Eddie’s problems, while integrating their contextual knowledge. Often, a nuanced understanding of the final line and its implications for the relationship was a key marker of a higher-level response.

72 Examiners felt that responses to 72 were generally stronger than in last year’s paper, with fewer candidates missing or offering very brief responses, which is encouraging. As always, choosing a poem that enables a clear focus on the theme was important, and examiners were pleased to report that the theme of relationships worked with a wide range of poems, with no single choice dominating. Most responses considered romantic relationships in poems such as “Valentine”, “Cozy Apologia” and “Sonnet 43”. …

Context was addressed with greater confidence, particularly in 71; however, there does still appear to be an issue with knowledge being demonstrated on the chosen poem – in this case Armitage’s “The Manhunt” – not being replicated across both questions.

c720u10-jun25-11-q:
The vast majority of candidates recognized the extract as coming from the opening scene of the play, with just a few believing it was from either Act 3 scene 1 or Act 5 Scene 3. Examiners felt that the question was extremely accessible, enabling responses to explore the anger and aggression of the heads of the feuding families, the contrasting responses of their wives, and the effect of the “ancient grudge” on the long-suffering citizens of Verona. The Prince’s speech, especially his final two lines, led many candidates to show their appreciation of the extract’s structural significance in setting up and foreshadowing later events.

8 Stronger responses often began by placing the extract, then considering the key ideas and viewpoints within it. They commented effectively on the urgency and violence shown in the first half, along with the Prince’s subsequent intervention and threat. Many tracked the extract successfully, with some seeing the humour created by the stage direction describing “old Capulet in his gown” demanding a longsword and Lady Capulet’s line “A crutch! A crutch! Why call you for a sword?” Others appreciated Shakespeare’s mirroring of characters in order to present the similarities between both sides of the feud. Weaker responses tended to neglect the Prince’s speech, or get sidetracked by the wives’ attempts to restrain their husbands’ violent urges into offering extended discussion of Elizabethan gender roles, usually at the expense of a sharper focus on the language and structure of the extract itself. While the Prince’s description of the families as “enemies to peace” and “beasts” often drew effective comments from candidates, examiners felt that equally useful phrases such as “quench the fire”, “purple fountains” and “bloody hands” were mostly overlooked. Overall, the main message from examiners was that a lack of focus on specific language choices inhibited marks more than any other factor.
c720u10-jun25-12-q:
This question on one of the play’s key themes proved accessible, with examiners reporting that it enabled a variety of approaches. While most started with the Prologue and the labelling of Romeo and Juliet as “star-crossed lovers”, then tracked the idea of fate across the play, others selected key moments that seemed to involve luck, mainly good luck, to bring about the meeting of Romeo and Juliet in Act 1 Scene 5 and then bad luck in the subsequent events that lead to their suicides. Some candidates explored the idea of free will and the extent to which certain characters such as Friar Lawrence and Romeo are responsible for their own actions in the play, despite blaming fate or misfortune. Examiners noted the fact that contextual details intruded less for this question than in recent years, and were limited to brief and reasonable mentions of Elizabethan ideas of fate and astrology.

Weaker responses tended to be narrative in nature and struggled to find clear focus on the key words in the question, perhaps inserting the words “fate” or “luck” rather tenuously. These often tried to fit in learned quotations that lacked relevance to the question. Examiners felt that such answers would have benefitted from a more selective approach, focusing on key moments where fate of luck could be seen to play a tangible part. Typically, the main limiting factor in less successful responses was a lack of engagement with language choices for AO2 marks. In more effective answers, examiners noted how apt quotations such as “I am fortunes fool”, “I defy you stars” and “a plague on both your houses” were used both to support points and enable effective word-level analysis. As ever, candidates who planned their responses often managed to produce more focused, coherent discussions. Those who looked at Romeo’s struggles with the machinery of fate and his ultimately futile attempts to alter his destiny often did well, usually selecting key moments such as the Prologue, Act 1 Scene 5, Act 3 Scene 1 and Act 5 Scene 3 to explore the theme. Friar Lawrence’s foreshadowing warnings to the doomed couple (for example “These violent delights have violent ends”) and Shakespeare’s use of celestial imagery also proved fruitful in addressing AO2 in the mark scheme.
c720u10-jun25-21-q:
Despite not directly featuring the play’s central characters, the dialogue between Lady Macduff and Ross in the extract presents the effects of Macbeth’s tyranny on a domestic level, and precedes a pivotal moment in the play that leads directly to his downfall. The majority of candidates recognized this, and most could track the conversation between the characters, with the accessibility of the language enabling them to probe linguistic and structural choices such as Lady Macduff’s use of questions, Ross’s triple-adjective defence of Macduff’s character (“noble, wise, judicious”) and key words such as “fly”, “fear” and “madness”. The contrast between Lady Macduff’s confusion and frustration at her husband’s sudden departure and Ross’s attempt at calm reassurance enabled candidates to make relevant points, and examiners were also able to reward comments on the second-hand presentation of Macduff (and indeed Macbeth) in the extract.

Better responses were usually informed by the scene’s dramatic irony, with the audience having recently been informed of Macbeth’s intentions to “give to th’edge of the sword (Macduff’s) wife, his babes”, and candidates that understood what happens shortly after Ross’s departure tended to empathise more fully with Lady Macduff’s distress. Examiners pointed to engagement with the image of the “poor wren” defending “her young ones in her nest, against the owl” as a key discriminator for higher bands; those that could go on to discuss the “wild and violent sea” of Macbeth’s reign often went on to reach the very top bands. Candidates that could see the breadth of Lady Macduff’s emotions were able to offer more detailed, thoughtful responses, while the few that questioned Ross’s early departure and his possible reasons for it impressed examiners. Less successful responses tended to lack an understanding of where the extract fits into the play, or neglected AO2 by passing up the opportunities to probe language choices. Some candidates seemed to answer as if they had simply misread “Lady Macduff” as “Lady Macbeth”, often tying themselves in knots trying to place this moment in her character arc. Overall, though, examiners felt that the biggest source of underachievement was the time wasted in offering sweeping and entirely unnecessary contextual comments on gender in Jacobean society, despite contextual understanding not being assessed in the Shakespeare questions.

Unfortunately, many examiners noted how Lady Macduff was the recipient of the kind of casual misogyny that has been directed at Lady Macbeth in recent series – apparently because she has the temerity to question why she and her family have been deserted by her husband just before they are brutally murdered. Examiners saw her described as “disrespectful”, “annoying”, “stupid” and “playing the victim”, while Ross was offered sympathy. While such views were difficult to support and therefore not easy to reward, the concerns here go far beyond the narrow confines of an extract question.
c720u10-jun25-22-q:
Examiners felt that this question was extremely accessible, allowing even the least confident of candidates to respond and achieve their potential. The opportunity to write about how the play’s title character changes was welcomed, and the question elicited a high number of sustained responses. Most candidates began with the Captain’s report of “brave” Macbeth’s exploits on the battlefield in Act 1 Scene 2 and tracked his changes across the play, with those that picked out key turning points gaining credit for the structural part of AO2 to add to their AO1 understanding. Many also noted Macbeth’s propensity for violence in that early scene, and were able to see this as Shakespeare foreshadowing his later fall into murderous tyranny. Most candidates saw the influence of the witches and Lady Macbeth as drivers of his changes, along with his own “vaulting ambition”. Examiners were impressed with the sheer range of quotations that had been learned by candidates to support their comments and enable language analysis across their answers.

12 Stronger responses tended to be selective in their choices of key moments where Macbeth changes, supporting their discussion with apt quotations that could then be probed for AO2 marks. They also managed to offer an overarching view of Macbeth, sometimes bringing in evidence from other characters’ perspectives on him, such as “something wicked this way comes” and “those he commands move only in command, nothing in love”. Candidates who saw Macbeth as a construct rather than just a man, and who offered a nuanced, evaluative view, inevitably reached the upper end of the mark scheme. In contrast, those that took a narrative approach with less of a focus on the specific changes Macbeth undergoes struggled to get out of Band 2, particularly if they neglected word-level language analysis. Examiners were frustrated when effective quotations had been learned and used as evidence, yet not mined for AO2 marks. Other key messages from examiners included how lengthy forays into contextual discussion, for example on James I’s obsession with the supernatural, Jacobean gender roles or the Gunpowder Plot, rarely added much to answers; also, they are less impressed by the showy use of niche technical terminology (this year’s favourite: chremamorphism) than revision websites might have you believe, especially when such terms are used incorrectly or lead to lengthy explanations of what they entail. As always, it is comment on the effects of devices and word choices that brings the best rewards for AO2.
c720u10-jun25-31-q:
Examiners felt that this was an extremely accessible extract, with almost all candidates able to place it within the play’s narrative and discuss the joy of Othello and Desdemona being reunited in Cyprus and how it its undercut by Iago’s ominous aside. Most candidates drew on the mirrored expressions of love in the shared line “O, my fair warrior!”, “My dear Othello!”, with some unpicking “fair warrior”, inferring Othello’s respect for Desdemona’s strength and seeing this as an equal, loving relationship. The pair’s hyperbolic exchange and public kiss provided material for discussion, although there were some misunderstandings prompted by Othello’s description of the height of the waves and Desdemona’s invocation of “the heavens”.

Less effective responses failed to pick up on the shift in tone towards the end of the extract when we are brought into Iago’s confidence with the aside. Some were distracted by Iago’s reference to “the Moor” at the start and wanted to discuss Iago’s racism, often linking this to unhelpful contextual comments. Some candidates managed Band 3 responses that would easily have reached Band 4 with a little more attention to AO2. Stronger answers sensed the foreboding references to death in Othello’s speech, noting that this moment marks the peak of Othello and Desdemona’s relationship, so the only way is down, signalled by Iago’s malevolent promise to the audience. Those that unpicked this metaphor (“I’ll set down the pegs that make this music”) tended to do well, often also noting the irony of Othello’s triumphant “our wars are done” just as a bigger battle is beginning.
c720u10-jun25-32-q:
Examiners were generally impressed with how well candidates responded to this relatively open question, and many enjoyed the freedom it afforded them: most wrote about racism or sexism in the play, with many discussing both; some candidates also discussed class prejudice. The majority of responses began with Iago and Roderigo’s late-night alarmist rousing of Brabantio, with “Even now, now, very now, an old black ram is tupping your white ewe” providing ample opportunity for AO2 analysis. Iago’s racism was explored, along with Brabantio’s accusation that Othello used enchantments to coerce Desdemona, the frequent use of “the Moor” and the Duke’s backhanded compliment that Othello is “far more fair than black”. Many candidates explored the misogyny that Desdemona, Emilia and Bianca suffer, with Iago’s view of women and treatment of Emilia prominent, along with how Desdemona is seen as Brabantio’s property at the start of the play and Cassio’s treatment of Bianca and description of her as a “bauble”.

Better responses were able to show strong focus on prejudice and explore its presentation and effects across the whole play. Examiners were particularly impressed with the good use of textual quotations as both effective support for discussion and material for close analysis of language and structure. Those that were able to explore Iago’s manipulation of Othello’s internalised racism and how this is used to change him did well, often offering well-chosen references in support. Similarly, candidates that tracked Emilia’s progression from pleasing Iago’s “fantasy” with the handkerchief, to trying to educate Desdemona about the realities for women in the world, to finally finding her voice to expose Iago – and dying for it – were usually very successful overall. Weaker responses tended to struggle with focus, mainly due to not fully understanding “prejudice” and getting it confused with jealousy, power or a general dislike. Other reasons for less successful responses were brevity, a lack of textual support or reluctance to address AO2.
c720u10-jun25-41-q:
This extract worked extremely well for all levels of ability, with almost all candidates recognising that it was the gulling of Beatrice, and the majority being able to place it accurately within the play’s events. Many commented on Shakespeare’s use of dramatic irony and saw the humour in Beatrice being tricked so easily. It was particularly pleasing to see how many candidates appreciated how we are presented with another side to Hero in this scene, with many commenting on the playfulness and intelligence she shows while she is away from the male characters. Most candidates began by discussing Ursula and Hero’s conversation, often exploring the hyperbole and complimentary language used to describe Benedick. This was usually followed by engagement with Beatrice’s soliloquy, with many viewing this as a turning point for Beatrice, as she finally accepts her underlying feelings for Benedick.

Stronger responses dealt with both halves of the extract, exploring the exaggeratedly positive language and imagery of Ursula and Hero’s discussion of Benedick’s qualities before considering Beatrice’s thoughts and feelings when alone at the end of the scene, often exploring the imagery of “taming” and the “fire” in her ears, and appreciating its structural importance to her relationship with Benedick. Less successful responses tended not to engage with Beatrice’s soliloquy, or struggled to appreciate the covert trickery of the conversation between Ursula and Hero. There was some misunderstanding, with some believing that Ursula is in love with Benedick; there was also frequent confusion over who or what is “prized”, with many believing that this word referred to Benedick rather than Beatrice’s wit. The most common reason for underachievement was a reluctance to engage with the rich language and imagery in the extract, thereby limiting AO2 marks.
c720u10-jun25-42-q:
Examiners reported that this question was generally handled well by candidates, with the concept of reputation clearly understood. A wide range of characters was discussed, most commonly Hero, Claudio, Don Pedro, Don John and Leonato, but also Beatrice, Benedick, and, occasionally, Dogberry. Reputation was interpreted in a variety of ways, encompassing ideas of honour, status, respectability, shame, slander and respect. Many discussed the lack of consistency and fairness around reputation, particularly regarding the female characters in the play and gender inequality. Context tended to creep in here, although in most cases without too much detrimental digression. The question leant itself to a non-chronological approach, which meant there were fewer narrative approaches than usual, and examiners noted that there were some confident links made to the title, and often thoughtful discussion of the unnecessary problems caused by the characters’ fixation with reputation. Unsurprisingly, Hero’s rejection at the altar was the moment most frequently discussed, providing candidates with plenty of textual references to work on for AO2 marks.

Better responses really explored the focus of the question: “the importance of reputation”, and were able to look evaluatively at its influence on characters and how it drives the plot. They tended to address AO2 both structurally, through discussion of dramatic irony, foreshadowing and turning points, and through language choices, with the contrasting imagery of the lamb and the lion used to describe Claudio and the connotations of Leonato’s view of Hero having fallen into “a pit of ink” proving particularly useful. Weaker responses tended to be brief, often only writing about Claudio and Hero, or showed confusion over plot, characters or quotations. Some took the gender-based aspects of reputation into extended explanation of the inequalities in Elizabethan England, thus losing focus and wasting precious time. As usual, most detrimental to marks was a lack of attention to AO2, often keeping marks at the lower end of Bands.
c720u10-jun25-51-q: It appears that no centres had taught this text for this series, meaning that responses examiners saw were the result of rubric infringements and therefore answered as unseen. This inevitably limited marks to the lower end of Band 2 or below.
c720u10-jun25-52-q: As previously noted, it appears no centres had taught this text for this series. However, examiners saw a small number of responses from candidates who clearly knew the text, perhaps from studying it at Key Stage 3 or another school. They were able to focus on the question and show understanding of characters and events, though were perhaps inevitably light on specific textual references, and thus struggled to register much in the way of AO2 marks.
c720u10-jun25-61-q:
The extract enabled engagement from candidates of all abilities, given that it is from early in the play, has a strong narrative element and is key to setting up the play’s plot. Candidates were generally empathetic towards Shylock’s position, but disapproved of his racist attitude, with some feeling that the extract itself gave a skewed impression of his character, while many saw this as the moment he is established as the play’s antagonist. His attitude towards Christians in general and Antonio in particular provided plenty of material for comment. Opinions on Bassanio’s attitude varied, with many feeling that his invitation to dinner was sincerely meant and an expression of goodwill; others saw duplicity, and an attempt to ingratiate himself with Shylock to secure the loan.

Weaker responses often failed to grasp the significance of Shylock’s aside or became too caught up in contextual explanation and comment, often at the expense of digging into the language and structure of the extract itself. A few candidates took their response beyond the extract, wasting valuable time that would have been more productively spent in analysing the dynamic between the three characters presented on the page. Quite a few candidates didn’t get as far as Antonio’s lines towards the end of the extract, so weren’t able to comment on his high-handed words regarding the loan. Better answers tended to do well on Shylock in particular, seeing the sharp contrast between his superficially polite speech towards Antonio and the deep hatred shown within the aside. For AO2, there were successful explorations of phrases such as “I will feed fat the ancient grudge”, “our sacred nation” and “cursed be our tribe”, and close engagement with language choice was often the mark of a more successful response.

Characteristics of good extract responses:

• Clear and sustained focus on the question asked and on the details in the extract. • “Placing” of the extract within the play’s events and giving some overview of its significance and key ideas. • Selection of short, apt references to support points made. • Critical probing of inferences, implicit meanings and subtext as well as more surface ideas. • Wide-ranging coverage of the extract. • Close examination of how the language/imagery used helps to convey meaning.

Ways in which performance could be improved:

• More detailed coverage of the extract, managing comment on the beginning, middle and end, not straying beyond it. • More selection of specific supporting references rather than general impressions. • Less reference to contextual factors when AO3 is not addressed in this question. • More practice on probing figurative language and connotations of key words to accumulate AO2 marks. • Practice in responding to both soliloquies and extracts with characters interacting and responding to each other.
c720u10-jun25-62-q:
This was an accessible question, and almost all candidates were able to respond, often at length, although examiners noted that many took a narrative-driven approach and struggled to get beyond Band 3, due to prioritising the re-telling of plot over evaluation of the relationship itself. Most candidates started with Bassanio’s description of Portia as “a lady richly left” and a “golden fleece” in Act 1 Scene 1, with some then picking up on Portia’s brief, approving comments on Bassanio in Act 1 Scene 3. From there, most looked at the casket scene, the courtroom and Portia’s trick with the ring. Many candidates explored the balance of power within the relationship – is Portia submissive, or is she subtly controlling? – or discussed whether Bassanio really loves Portia, or marries her for purely mercenary reasons.

14 Better responses were evaluative, selecting key events involving the characters and exploring the fluctuating dynamic between them. Crucially, they were able to address AO2 through a combination of structural awareness and analysis of key words and images in relevant textual references. Some candidates compared them with other romantic relationships in the play, Nerissa and Gratiano, and Jessica and Lorenzo, with some success. Weaker answers tended to be narrative-focused, offering generalised statements, often without much attention to AO2; sometimes there were confusions with character or plot. Examiners felt that many responses could have been improved with more incorporation of specific textual detail in order to develop ideas further and provide more material for language analysis.

Characteristics of good essay responses:

• Close tracking of a character / relationship / theme across the whole text. • Selection of a range of apt events and specific details to support thoughtful ideas. • Probing of linguistic and structural choices in quotations used to support points. • Some analysis of the writer’s intentions when creating characters and plots. • Highlighting of important turning points and key contrasts and their effects. • Careful spelling and punctuation, with vocabulary and sentence structure used to control meaning effectively.

Ways in which performance could be improved:

• Tracking a character / relationship / theme across the whole text, with effective coverage of the play. • More focus on including short quotations that can be analysed for AO2; fewer contextual comments. • Practice in creating clear, cohesive arguments which address the question posed. • Practice in selecting detailed textual evidence for ideas. • Practice in proof-reading responses to avoid technical errors, such as forgetting use of capital letters for character names, neglecting punctuation and abbreviating character names.
c720u10-jun25-71-q:
This question on the presentation of love in Duffy’s Valentine enabled almost all candidates to respond, and examiners felt that it was accessible for the whole ability range. Many understood that the speaker is rejecting stereotypical, commercialized Valentine’s gifts, along with some of the traditional conventions of love poetry, while offering a more honest representation of love. Candidates were able to engage with the ideas and language of the poem through the extended metaphor of the onion, with the majority probing the connotations of phrases such as “a moon wrapped in brown paper”, “fierce kiss” and “cling to your knife”, and this meant that AO2 marks could be accumulated by many. Despite being pleased to see so much engagement with the poem, examiners felt that interpretations were sometimes rather skewed, noting that a significant minority of responses suggested that Duffy is rejecting love itself, or focused almost entirely on the darker second half of the poem without seeing the “light”, or appreciating the poem’s more playful moments. Similarly, some examiners were uncomfortable with biographical context that either seemed to make dubious assertions about Duffy’s love life or simplistic links between her sexuality and the “weird gift” of the onion. Overall, a relative lack of meaningful context was the most limiting factor here, with social, cultural, historical and literary connections generally more effective than biographical ones.

Stronger responses were able to offer some overview of the key ideas about how love is presented in the poem, and took full advantage of the poem’s accessible yet rich language to address AO2. Examiners noted that structural comments were more meaningful than usual, with Duffy’s use of free verse, repetition and single line / word stanzas eliciting some thoughtful comments. Careful tracking through the poem, noting the shifts in tone, enabled some to achieve sustained, engaged commentaries, particularly when linked to appropriate contextual details.

Even the weakest candidates were able to say something about the presentation of love, such as how both an onion and a loving relationship have layers; however, less successful responses tended to be brief and thin, usually omitting context and struggling to probe language choices. Candidates who saw the poem as a portrayal of a “toxic relationship”, rather than a presentation of the realities of love that any of us might experience, tended to limit themselves.

Examiners were pleased to report that a wide range of comparison poems worked well for this question. The most popular choices were poems that feature romantic love and relationships, primarily “Sonnet 43” and “Cozy Apologia”, closely followed by “The Manhunt”, “She Walks in Beauty”, “A Wife in London” and “Afternoons”. Love of nature was explored in “Death of a Naturalist” and “To Autumn”, love of country in “The Soldier” and self-love in “Ozymandias”. c720u10-nov21-11-q:
The paper did its job well, with no questions misleading or confusing candidates: the extracts seemed familiar to candidates and the essay questions appeared accessible. There were, however, a number of rubric infringements, with a few candidates missing out questions and a couple attempting to answer all of the Shakespeare extracts. These didn’t seem to be a result of any issues with the questions, though, and, as with last year’s November paper, were more likely to be a consequence of disruption to learning and the length of time that had elapsed between candidates studying the plays and sitting the exam.

Responses ranged across all 5 bands, although a large majority tended to fall within bands 2 and 3, probably as a consequence of the unusual nature of this resit exam. Almost all candidates answered on “Macbeth” (the most popular of the Shakespeare texts) and “Romeo and Juliet”, and were able to access the questions and show engagement with the plays to at least some degree.

Comments on individual questions/sections

For question 1.1 candidates were able to discuss this key moment in Romeo and Juliet’s relationship, most commenting on how the characters’ willingness to abandon their family names showed the conviction of their sudden love and willingness to disregard their families’ feud. Some, however, didn’t seem to realise that Juliet only becomes aware of Romeo’s presence halfway through the extract, thus missing the dramatic irony of Juliet’s words. Better responses were able to track through the whole extract, offering some analysis of language choice, such as their use of religious imagery, while weaker ones tended to offer a couple of textual selections and more generalised comments on the lovers.

There were plenty of Capulet family relations available for candidates responding to question 1.2 to select from, but most wanted to write about Lord Capulet, whether in relation to Juliet, Tybalt or his wife. Some stronger responses looked at Capulet’s treatment of his daughter across several scenes in the play, selecting apt textual detail from each for analysis, thus ensuring good marks across both assessment objectives. There were also a few effective discussions of Juliet’s close relationship with the Nurse, sometimes contrasted with the more distant and uneasy relationship with her mother. Weaker responses identified one or two key elements of relationships but were brief or limited in scope and textual support.

Most candidates seemed familiar with the extract in question 2.1 and many were able to place it accurately within the play’s main events. Stronger responses looked at the widening gap between the Macbeths and explored the language suggestive of Macbeth’s mental deterioration. Some saw Lady Macbeth’s attempts to cheer her husband as evidence of their remaining love and interpreted it as a further example of her manipulation of him. On the whole, I felt that more could have been done to explore key images such as “We have scorched the snake” and “O full of Scorpions is my mind, dear wife!”, and a lack of attention to AO2 often characterised less successful responses.

Summary of key points

• Rubric infringements are always costly: missing out a question on this component has a major impact on overall marks and, ultimately, grades. Attempting extract or essay questions on plays that have not been studied rarely achieves anything other than wasting valuable time that could have been used more productively on persisting with a single extract and essay response.

• For essay questions, AO2 needs to be addressed through selection and analysis of key textual references, or comments on the play’s structure, for example looking at contrasts, cause and effect and how plot and character development relates to the play’s overall shape.

c720u10-nov21-71-q:
A statistically small cohort of candidates responded to the paper set in this series. Centres and candidates should be commended for submitting a range of responses which reflected secure reading and understanding of texts in challenging circumstances. It was clear from the responses seen that some candidates did not have the necessary exam stamina required to produce detailed and sustained responses in comparison to previous cohorts. A significant majority of responses demonstrated secure Band 3 skills, with a smaller number of candidates demonstrating the skills required to secure Band 4 which may of course be due to a range of factors including the current Covid context.

The questions worked across all texts for all abilities. At the lower end, there was a tendency towards unfocused narrative but most candidates attempted to deal with the characters or themes reflected in the questions set and the majority of candidates produced focused and supported essays. There was clear engagement with the texts and the questions set.

All the extracts worked well as a starting point for candidates and they were, quite rightly, used in different ways. Some candidates included the extract at the start of their response; many used the extract as part of a chronological approach; and others used it throughout their response, cross referenced with the wider text. All approaches were valid and all were able to work satisfactorily for the individual candidates concerned. Very few didn’t use the extract at all, though some treated it with a light touch, preferring to focus on the wider text. This too was acceptable, although potentially a wasted opportunity. A number of candidates made no, or very little reference to the wider text and relied solely on the extract. Overall, the questions across all the texts worked well for all abilities.

The majority of candidates answered the question set on An Inspector Calls with a smaller number answering the question set on Blood Brothers.

Comments on individual questions/sections

c720u10-nov21-78-q:
The question’s focus, on the character of Sheila Birling, worked well and led to many focused and engaged responses. The question enabled more able students to comment in detail on the breadth of the play while less able candidates demonstrated a straightforward knowledge of events and related these to Sheila’s role in the investigation of Eva Smith’s death.

Candidates often started with a focus on Sheila’s attitudes in the extract before broadening out to reference how these change in the rest of the play. The extract was a convenient starting point to discuss the events involving Sheila and Eva Smith at Milwards, before broadening discussion out to Sheila’s changing attitudes in recounting the events and how these are consolidated in the rest of the play. In terms of AO2, the extract gave students the opportunity to provide a close analysis of the language and there was much discussion of stage directions such as when the character “almost breaks down” and reacts “stormily” to Eric. Indeed, the final part of the extract was well used and provided a useful starting point for a discussion of Sheila’s relationship with her family and Gerald Croft, with better candidates discussing how these change throughout the play.

Weaker candidates relied heavily or solely on the extract, often providing a focused analysis of details from the extract without addressing the wider text. Lower band answers also tended to bolt on discussion of Priestley’s intentions in writing the play without linking to characters and events.

Very few candidates attempted this text. Candidates took a range of varied, valid approaches to the question and reference to the extract provided. Overall responses were relatively short and lacked sustained development and detailed support from the text however candidates successfully focused and commented on the character of Edward. Some responses used a comparative approach to focus on Edward in contrast to Mickey which was valid and allowed candidates to demonstrate knowledge of the text and major plot points. Responses showed a clear understanding of Edward’s relationship with both Mrs Lyons and Mrs Johnstone and Mickey. A few responses also commented successfully on Edward’s relationship with Linda. Very few responses commented on the ending of the play.

Summary of key points

Points to remember:

• The first key question for the examiner is: ‘Does the candidate know the text well?’ • The second key question for the examiner is: ‘Has the candidate answered the question in a focused and sustained way?’

Characteristics of good essay responses: • Clear and sustained focus on the question asked • Use of the extract at a relevant point of the essay • Selection of short references to support points made • Coverage and reference to a range of relevant points across the wider text

• Critical probing of inferences, implicit meanings and subtext as well as more surface ideas • Close analysis of how the language and writer’s techniques in the extract and wider text help to present the focus of the question • Suitable analytical style of writing.

Ways in which performance could be improved: • Plan where coverage of the extract will be best placed in the essay • More detailed coverage of the extract and wider text, including the beginning, middle and end • More selection of detailed supporting references rather than general impressions • Avoid unfocused narrative and retelling of the story • More practice on subtext and interpretation • Practise creating clear, cohesive arguments which address the question asked • Avoid reference to plays and films when discussing prose texts • Practise and develop an analytical style of essay writing.
