Some of the best responses often included assured and sensitive discussion of Godfrey within the wider framework of his relationships not just with Nancy but with his father and brother and drew on the influence his childhood had on him in all subsequent relationships.

There was often thoughtful discussion about Godfrey and Nancy’s childlessness and attempt to reclaim Eppie leading to conclusions about the relative importance (or insignificance) of money. Many candidates traced Godfrey’s growth through the novel, with original and insightful evaluations of his character and the influence Nancy had upon his character development.

AO3 was well discussed and mostly perceptive and assured. The vast majority provided excellent examples of integrated discussion on historical context (e.g., poverty and the value of family in contrast to monetary wealth) while some candidates commented on the novel’s links to religious beliefs, families, Victorian expectations and the contrast between social classes. Candidates also discussed attitudes towards children born out of wedlock, the lack of a maternal figure in the Cass household and Godfrey’s changing attitudes and redemption often within the wider context of attitudes to religion and forgiveness.
c720u20-jun23-23-q:
The question asked candidates to consider the ways the Martian invasion causes law and order to break down in the novel. The extract focused on the Narrator’s brother rescuing the Elphinstones from three men attempting to steal their pony and chaise. Some candidates seemed unfamiliar with the extract and got a bit muddled over the word ‘fugitives’, which many took to mean ‘escaped prisoners’ rather than ‘people running away’. Many more though, placed the extract well as part of the brother’s narrative perspective and were able to examine the rich AO2 in pleasing detail, particularly examining the violent nature of verbs such as, “slashed”, “struck” and “gripped”. Occasionally, the use of “whip” was linked to how the Martians had enslaved humans like animals as law and order broke down, which was quite a thoughtful point for those that made it. Often, much was made of the “pugilistic chivalry”, leading to discussion around attitudes to women at the time and how the invasion had led to a breakdown of this aspect of order in society.

29 Discussion of the wider text often successfully focussed on Wells’ descriptions of the panic and violence that broke out following the invasion, often with very perceptive selection of key moments from the “Exodus” section of the novel. Lower band responses were quite generalised and commented on ways in which, “there was panic”, or how, “violence broke out”, but these comments were not always then linked to specific characters or incidents.

Many candidates sensibly used the question to focus on key minor characters and show how the breakdown in law and order is presented through the Curate and the Artilleryman. These were often linked well to AO3 points of context and led to discussion on how they represent Wells’ critical views on Victorian pillars of society such as the Church and the Military, as well as valid references to the survival of the fittest; Tasmania; the British Empire; and Imperialism which were all often skillfully used.
c720u20-jun23-24-q:
Pride and Prejudice proved to be relatively popular once again and was studied right across the ability range. Candidates studying this text responded well to the opportunities offered by the novel and the set question, which called on candidates to consider the turning points in Elizabeth and Darcy’s relationship in the novel. Fewer candidates relied solely on the extract with only very brief reference to the rest of the text and more candidates tracked fully to the end of the novel. Responses were discursive and though there was increased specific support from the text (either paraphrased reference to events or direct supporting reference) this remains an area to develop and improve. Most candidates were able to place the extract precisely in the timeline of events. Many responses unfortunately remained overly reliant on film adaptations of the novel and took a narrative approach which lacked depth and detail of direct evidence/quotation from the text.

The extract allowed many candidates to discuss both characters and their attitudes to marriage, prejudice, and social status; however overall, there was limited exploration of AO2.

Many candidates discussed Darcy and Elizabeth’s relationship and route to marriage in contrast to the marriage between Mr Collins and Charlotte Lucas which was often somewhat forced into responses. More successful responses used the contrast between Charlotte’s marriage as a springboard to discuss marriage within the wider text linking it to Elizabeth’s expectations, prospects of marriage, rejection of marriage proposals and eventual marriage to Darcy. The top band answers framed discussion of Darcy and Elizabeth’s unconventional courtship within the wider frame of Austen’s presentation of women, marriage, status and class. Most candidates included reference to Darcy’s early opinions and prejudice towards Elizabeth and vice-versa and often tracked skilfully through the turning points in their relationship. A significant number of responses focused only on Darcy’s proposals, missing opportunities to discuss turning points as indicated in the question. The best answers linked discussion with AO3 context points seamlessly woven in, through comments on the social and economic standing of Darcy and Elizabeth, their respective behaviour, demeanour and attitudes to marriage in the novel. Comments on structural features such as the use of letters in the novel were commented on by a minority of candidates to help illustrate the turning points of Darcy and Elizabeth’s relationship.

Centres should remind candidates to express their ideas and comments using a suitable style and tone and avoid oversimplifications such as Mr. Darcy “catches feelings for Liz”.
c720u20-jun23-25-q:
Jane Eyre continues to be relatively popular once again, with a fair ability range amongst candidates. This open question focused on conflict between the characters in the novel and this allowed the majority of candidates to provide assured, confident and evaluative discussion.

The extract was taken from near the start of the novel and saw the first physical and mental conflict that Jane endured, so it was understandable that the vast majority of the candidates used it as a starting point for their discussions. The extract allowed for perceptive discussion of AO2 features such as John Reed’s imperative language and the violent lexis such as, “cut”, “pain” and “hurl”. This often led to discussion of Jane’s time in the red room (with all its metaphorical and symbolic interpretations) and Jane’s inferior societal position as a “dependent”.

A common approach for many candidates was to track the places Jane spent her life and reference the conflict she suffered in these places. As a result, there was much appropriate discussion of Jane’s conflict with the Reeds, Mr Brocklehurst, Rochester and St John. Often, these were done in detailed, thoughtful and perceptive ways. A significant number of responses sensibly featured detailed reference to Bertha Mason’s treatment and this was often used as an opportunity to skillfully weave in AO3 references to gender, religion, economic status, social class and sensitive parallels between Jane and the real-life situation of Charlotte Brontë.

Overall, this was a very successful question for the candidates who studied the novel.
c720u20-jun23-26-q:
The question focused on the ways Stevenson creates fear at different points in the novel and worked well. All candidates were able to incorporate their knowledge of plot and character and respond to the question in a variety of valid ways. Most candidates were aided by the extract and referred to the pathetic fallacy, “deserted” streets of London and the distress of Poole and Jekyll’s servants and how they were used by Stevenson to create fear. Film versions seemed to be less prevalent this year, though were still occasionally present. Candidates engaged fully with the extract, discussion of which at times, also led to full coverage of the text and Jekyll/Hyde’s eventual death. Much was made of the atmosphere, the weather, the moon and the way the servants were “huddled together like a flock of sheep”. Candidates also commented on the fear of Poole, Utterson and the servants and the way they speak and behave in the extract.

The majority of responses referenced key aspects of the wider text e.g., Jekyll’s scientific experimentation or “heresies” and Hyde’s character. Many invariably cited Hyde’s “troglodytic” appearance, “ape like fury” and “Satan’s signature” to target AO2. Candidates often widened the scope of their discussions to consider the murder of Sir Danvers Carew and Lanyon’s death. The top band responses widened their scope further with some nuanced and sensitive discussion of Utterson’s gradual discoveries and Jekyll’s fear and dread over what he has become in his transformative state. There was also some sensitive discussion of the way different points of view and first-person narratives, such as the accounts left by Dr Lanyon and Dr Jekyll, added to the growing fear. Some candidates surprisingly did not mention Hyde which limited their responses significantly. Many candidates did not refer to the main concept of the novel and the fear associated with transforming from one person into another or, despite the extract, to Jekyll’s death at the end of the novel. Candidates should be reminded to discuss the main concepts of the text.

31 On the whole, the use of context was secure, relevant and accurate and at its best, well developed and sensitively applied. Occasionally candidates used context to drive their essays, and whilst this can be a valid approach, it often limited reference to the whole text. There was again less use of biographical information about Stevenson ‘bolted-on’. There was also less reliance on discussions of Freud and the id and ego theories, both of which allowed candidates to focus more fully on events in the text. Better approaches tended to include discussion of the text linked to the ideas of Victorian societal expectations, respectability, repression and hypocrisy; Darwin’s Theory of Evolution; the conflict between science and religion; the Victorian fascination with physiognomy; and links to contemporary literary trends all of which could be directly linked to, and exemplified by, textual details.

Summary of Key Points

Points to remember: • the first key question for the examiner is: ‘Does the candidate know the text well?’ • the second key question for the examiner is: ‘Has the candidate answered the question in a focused and sustained way?’ • AO2 and AO3 are worth a third of the marks but are not expected to take up a third of the essay • responses must be legible.

Characteristics of good Section B essay responses: • clear and sustained focus on the question asked • use of the extract at a relevant point of the essay • appropriate selection of short references to support points made • coverage and reference to a range of relevant points across the wider text • critical probing of inferences, implicit meanings and subtext as well as more surface ideas • close analysis of how the language, writer’s techniques in the extract and wider text help to present the focus of the question • clear appreciation of how contextual factors influence characters and themes • suitable analytical style of writing.

Ways in which performance could be improved: • plan where coverage of the extract will be best placed in the essay • more detailed coverage of the extract and wider text, including the beginning, middle and end • more selection of detailed supporting references rather than general impressions • avoid unfocused narrative and retelling of the story • more practice on exploring subtext and interpretation • practise creating clear, cohesive arguments which address the question asked • more focused and integrated discussion of how contextual factors influence writers’ characters, themes and ideas. Avoid contextual ‘bolt-ons’ • careful adherence to the rubric requirements of the paper to ensure that candidates are only answering questions on the texts that they have studied • avoid reference to plays and films when discussing prose texts • practise and develop an analytical style of essay writing.
c720u20-jun23-31-q:
Nettles was accessible to the vast majority of candidates. The relatively straightforward narrative meant that most candidates identified that the poem was about a young boy falling into nettles, being comforted by the father who then cut down the nettles. Many related to their own experiences with nettles and empathised greatly with the child.

Candidates often focussed on the father’s love for his son and their close relationship; with a majority also exploring the violent war-like imagery. Perceptive responses intertwined these two ideas and explored how the war imagery arose from the father’s love. There was much discussion of the bed image, usefully explored by the persona in the poem itself.

Whilst most candidates were able to understand the ending, in which the nettles grow back and the child is potentially hurt by them again, better candidates tended to offer a deeper meaning that the father would not always be able to protect the son, that the son was going to encounter further, more serious hurt in the future.

Inevitably, some candidates proposed that the poem was actually about a real war, with a number of responses promoting this idea at the expense of full engagement with the poem. There were a number of responses which suggested that the nettles symbolised school bullies or decided that the child had died and the parent was holding a vigil for them.

33 On the whole though, this poem was well received, and most candidates were able to produce a relevant response.
c720u20-jun23-32-q:
The pairing of Nettles and Swimming with Aidan, aged 4 gave the candidates plenty to discuss in terms of comparison and worked well across the entire ability range. As the more challenging poem, candidates were generally less secure with the second poem compared to the first, but most were able to grasp the main key ideas of the poem. Some of this may have been due to timing issues.

The best candidates fully understood the father’s relationship with his son and the poignancy of the final lines. Many appreciated that Aiden “struggled more” with life in general compared to when he was in the pool, with some thoughtful appreciation of the choice of the word “magic”. There was often good appreciation of the alliterative “grace, grit, guts and get- me gusto”, successfully linking this with the power of Aidan in the pool. There were some lovely interpretations of the title, with some linking it to something akin to a label in a photo album and a snapshot of a moment in time. Recognition of the pride concerning Aidan’s accomplishments against other children tended to signify a top band candidate.

There was real engagement through interpretations of the father’s relationship with his son. Some candidates read the poem as the father being overcritical of his son and highlighting all his faults to encourage him to be independent. Other thoughtful responses suggested that Aiden might have some kind of disability or be autistic, which were well supported by close reference to the poem. There were also inevitable confusions. A number of candidates thought that this was Aiden’s first swimming lesson and that he was not very good at it.

Even the weakest candidates made a link in the mention of the two children’s ages. There was also a significant recognition of the children’s physical imperfections, with “blisters” linked to “scabs”. Many successfully linked the physical pain of the child in the first poem with the more emotional pain of the child in the second. Responses often discussed the character of each boy, with some saying that Aiden was far braver and more adventurous than the son in Nettles, others that they were both clumsy. Whilst these tended to be the most obvious/straightforward comparisons, some candidates were able to explore these in great depth and on a more sophisticated level.

The comparisons were often illuminating and, given that hardly anyone sitting the paper would have been a parent, there was some remarkable understanding of parental concern and guilt.

Overall, candidates gave every impression of having enjoyed writing about the poems and levels of engagement were very high.

Summary of Key Points

Characteristics of good poetry responses: • a thorough examination of the first poem in 3.1 • a thorough examination of the second poem in 3.2, either as a discrete element or as part of the comparison • recognition of the stated overview of the poems (found underneath the question on the paper) • clear comparison of ideas, mood and some reference to how the poets use language • detailed selection and coverage from each poem with supporting comments exploring the meaning and effects of these selections.

34 Ways in which performance can be improved: • ensure that the first poem is adequately analysed in 3.1 • ensure that the second poem is adequately analysed in depth in 3.2 • practise commenting on a range of poems and poetic techniques, including imagery and figurative language • avoid spotting and labelling techniques and patterns with no reference to meaning • develop the use of supporting references to support understanding of subtext • avoid ‘over reading’ of hidden meanings in the poems • gain experience in reading poems where similar topics are handled differently by poets • rehearse timings across the exam to ensure sufficient time is given to the poetry • make sure a range of comparative points are made in 3.2 • responses must be legible.
c720u20-jun24-01-q:
The extract proved to be very accessible and a good opportunity to discuss Jack’s importance to the novel. Many candidates made good use of the extract to comment on Golding’s increasingly animalistic and predatory description of Jack as “dog-like…on all fours”, “naked”, “down like a sprinter”, “crouched”. Many candidates used this as a springboard into thoughtful discussions of how the extract demonstrates Jack’s later near- animal behaviour commenting on his closeness to the ground, his connection to nature, the damage the island has done to his body and his ‘nearly mad’ eyes. Many candidates also commented on how Golding develops the presentation of Jack’s increasingly feral behaviours as the novel progresses.

In the wider text, candidates made good points about Jack’s arrival (and the symbolism of his clothes), his connection to Castle Rock, his initial friendship with Ralph and hatred of Piggy, his increasing volatility and then eventual violence and destructive mastery of the island. Not many handled the final scene on the beach, but those who did usually managed to write perceptively about the subtext and Golding’s moral messages too. The most successful responses also discussed Jack’s character in relation to the pursuit of power and fall of civilisation in the novel.
c720u20-jun24-02-q: Nearly all responses were rubric infringements that tackled the extract and question as ‘unseen’ with very little knowledge or understanding of the way Syal presents Anita’s character in the novel. However, the extract provided a rich opportunity to explore the presentation of character even when responses appeared to be attempting the question as unseen. Candidates focused on Anita’s “complete lack of emotion or indeed, social graces”, the way she “grunted” and “stifled a yawn”. Indeed, even candidates who seemed to tackle this without prior knowledge of the text were able to gain a little credit by discussing the extract and the character. Most responses, however, did not discuss other evidence or events from the wider text.
c720u20-jun24-03-q:
This is the last time Never Let Me Go will be examined on this particular specification, as it has been replaced by Boys Don’t Cry by Malorie Blackman.

The question elicited some thoughtful and sensitive discussions of Ruth’s character in the novel. There were also a significant number of rubric infringement responses where candidates had clearly not read the text but responded to the extract. The extract proved to be very accessible and a good opportunity to discuss Ruth’s reaction to her “possible”. Many candidates sensibly dealt with the extract by placing it after a discussion of Ruth’s earlier experience of Hailsham (including her bossy nature and lies about the pencil case) and her relationships with other characters. Many candidates also explored the more complex aspects of Ruth’s character in more detail including the time in the cottages, and in the lead up to her death. Weaker responses tended to make sweeping statements about Ruth’s character with little discussion of the latter stages of the novel.
c720u20-jun24-04-q:
The question provided candidates with the opportunity to discuss the woman in black, Jennet Humfrye, in detail. On the whole, candidates understood the character and her story well. Most candidates used the extract effectively to analyse Hill’s use of imagery in describing the woman as “dressed in deepest black”, “mourning”, “extremely pale” , and as “a victim of starvation”. A surprisingly large minority forgot to mention that she is, in fact, a ghost. She was described as ‘ghost-like’, ‘deathly’, ‘dead-looking’, ‘so ill looking she looks near dead’ but not often actually as a ghost.

Using the extract to comment on the woman’s appearances at Alice Drablow’s funeral then led many candidates to use this as a springboard to continue discussion of further events at Eel Marsh House, her backstory and revenge, the impact she has on Arthur Kipps and his beliefs and the deaths of Stella and Joseph at the end of the novel.

Film references are a particular issue for a significant minority of candidates, especially as they often deviate dramatically from the events of the novel. More selective use of the film version as a teaching aid is probably advisable.
c720u20-jun24-05-q:
Jeanette’s character is central to the novel and the vast majority of candidates engaged well with the question. Most candidates commented on Jeanette’s increasing independence and changing relationship with Mrs Winterson, with the best responses providing very detailed and nuanced examinations of this. Many candidates also included discussion of Jeanette’s relationships with other characters such as Elsie, Melanie and Katy and her changing views on religion and the Elim Pentecostal Church . The extract provided a rich opportunity to discuss Jeanette’s increasingly independent character. Those that used the extract well noted Winterson’s presentation of Jeanette’s thinking and emotions in the scene e.g. “I breezed in with more bravado than courage”, “In fact I was scared to death”, “I knew I had to be hard and white”, “It was not judgement day, but another morning”. Many responses also commented on the use of humour in the extract and wider novel such as, “I’m not havin’ demons here” and “all my relatives …were revolting”.

It was also pleasing to note the frequent purposeful references to the mythic elements of the novel, with these allegorical elements used to support the best responses. Many were also able to comment on the reconciliation between Jeanette and Mrs Winterson at the end of the novel. Weaker candidates struggled to include a range of detail from across the whole text.
c720u20-jun24-06-q:
The question, on the discovery of truths in the play, was very successful in providing the opportunity for some very detailed and perceptive responses from stronger candidates. It enabled them to evaluate how the discovery of truths and the subsequent fallout from them enabled Christopher to develop as a character. Understandably, the discovery of Judy’s letters to Christopher often played a central role in candidates’ essays.

Many candidates commented successfully on the extract, in particular the list-like repetition of, “Then I detected in…”, the listing of items discovered and the importance of “finding the shirt box” and subsequently Judy’s letters. There was some interesting discussion about how the first person / monologue structure of much of the play was used to present Christopher’s thoughts and feelings and the discovery of truths with extra impact for the audience.

30 Candidates who study this play really seem to engage and connect with it, and answers don’t tend to contain the ‘bolted on’ context (not assessed) that some of the other text choices in Section A seem to attract. However, there were a significant number of weaker responses where candidates either copied the extract completely, or copied large chunks of the extract without making any comment.
c720u20-jun24-07-q:
This is the last time A Taste of Honey will be examined on this particular specification, as it has been replaced by Leave Taking by Winsome Pinnock.

The extract provided a good basis for some very confident and sensitive responses about Helen’s character. Many candidates commented on key moments such as Helen’s reaction to Jo’s pregnancy and the way she reacts to and treats Geof. Some candidates also discussed the presentation of Helen as a mother and her relationship with Jo and her relationships with men such as Peter and the tension between her and Geof.

AO2 was tackled well by many candidates by focusing on Helen’s reaction to Peter, “Oh! My God! Look what the wind’s blown in” and her behaviour towards Jo, “go see to that coffee!”, “Turn yourself into a bloody termite and crawl into the wall… make yourself scarce”. The most assured responses also commented on Helen’s sarcasm and the witty dialogue of different exchanges in the play.

Weaker candidates lacked broader reference to the wider events in the play and stayed within the focus of the extract. There were fewer instances than previously of candidates referencing the 1961 film version rather than the original text, which cannot be valued as textual support by the examiner. Weaker responses also tend to focus on earlier events in greater detail and lose sight of the final scenes. As with other Section A texts, context can be problematic as ‘bolted on’ context or extended discussion about the characteristics of a kitchen sink drama, for example, are often unhelpful.
c720u20-jun24-08-q:
Candidates of all abilities were able to discuss Mr. Birling and his importance to the play as a whole. The vast majority were able to engage with the extract and demonstrate secure knowledge of the wider text.

A range of valid approaches was used. Some candidates chose to write about the extract first, tracking through to show Mr. Birling’s contributions to the extract. Given the extract’s position at the end of the play, many candidates understandably chose to explore it at the end of their essays, having dealt with the events of the wider text as they unfold chronologically in the play.

Successful responses focussed on specific examples of what Mr. Birling says and does in the course of the play and what this tells the audience about his character. Some key features of his personality were thoughtfully discussed and considered. These included his arrogance and self-belief as a “hard-headed man of business”; his over-confidence; his lack of respect for others (particularly the lower classes) and his desire to prove his status to others, such as Gerald or the Inspector. There was much discussion of the character’s early speeches and the Inspector’s refusal to be intimidated by Birling was very often evidenced by the quote, “I don’t play golf.”

31 Candidates often made relevant AO2 points by analysing the language used by the author in relation to Mr. Birling in the extract. Many candidates used this evidence to analyse how Birling was purely focused on his social status and reputation, rather than the death of Eva and accepting responsibility. In the wider text, candidates commonly referenced Mr. Birling’s role in aiding Priestley’s perceived intentions in writing the play. There were many references to Birling’s Titanic and World War comments and more able candidates were able to reference the stage directions in relation to Mr. Birling.

More able candidates sometimes discussed other characters and linked them successfully to Mr. Birling’s reactions and attitudes. Sensibly, many candidates discussed Eric and his relationship with his father. This often was used to springboard into a discussion on a contrast between the older and younger generations. Less able candidates sometimes took a narrative approach, and these responses did not always focus on Mr. Birling specifically, so were self-penalising.

Although context is not rewarded in Section A of this component, it understandably has an integral part to play in the teaching of this text. The majority of candidates made at least a passing reference to Capitalism and Socialism. However, occasionally, this led to lengthy paragraphs on these concepts that added little to the candidate’s overall mark. There was sometimes confusion over the time period of the play’s setting.

AO4 is assessed in this question. As always, there were many variations of the spelling of Priestley and Sheila and many instances of not using capital letters for proper nouns, e.g. Titanic.

Overall, this text continues to remain the most popular of the Section A texts and has proven once again to be engaging and accessible to the complete ability range of candidates.
c720u20-jun24-09-q:
Responses to this text were, on the whole, of a very high standard and it seems to be a text that is well chosen by centres who know their candidates’ ability to respond sensitively to its humour, themes and messages. There was some excellent analysis of the extract which provided a useful way into discussion of Hector in the wider text.

Candidates were well prepared to discuss Hector’s character in the extract and wider play. Most responses used the extract to evaluate AO2 and the presentation of Hector’s teaching of, “compound adjectives”, the “best moments in reading…” and references to Hardy, Larkin and Shakespeare. Most responses moved beyond the extract to evaluate key moments such as Hector’s role-play in lessons, teaching literature by heart, the significance of his motorcycle, his crash and memorial. Candidates also commented successfully on his relationship with the boys and other characters and made contrasts between his approach to education and that of Irwin and the Headteacher. On the whole candidates commented sensitively on Hector’s inappropriate behaviour and other character’s response to this.

Fewer candidates discussed the ending of the play in terms of what happens to the teachers and the boys and centres should remind students to comment on texts in full. Weaker responses tended to over-simplify and be a little formulaic in their assessment of Hector’s character. These responses tended to include quotes that contained the swear words contained in the play.
c720u20-jun24-10-q:
The question worked extremely well across the full range of abilities. All candidates, regardless of ability, had a very good knowledge of Mrs Johnstone’s character and the play as a whole. Many candidates discussed a selection of key moments such as Mrs Johnstone’s decision to “give” a child to Mrs Lyons, her superstitious nature, her relocation/new start, the confrontation with Mrs Lyons, her conversations with Edward, her support of Mickey and Linda and her attempts to intervene at the end of the play. Many candidates also successfully commented on events by framing their discussion around the presentation of Mrs Johnstone as a single mother, giving up and raising her children, and her moving on in the later stages of the play.

Many candidates commented on Russell’s use of language to present Mrs Johnstone in the extract and wider play such as her involvement with “the Welfare”; her reaction to Mrs Lyons’s suggestion, “What?”, and her hesitation in disclosing details, “Erm, well”; and seeming dismissal of the plan, “Oh, it’s mad...”. Many candidates commented on the use of stage directions and the narrator for dramatic effect such as, “How quickly an idea, planted can take root” … the thought “grew as surely as a seed in a mother’s womb”.

Context is obviously not explicitly rewarded here and while some stronger candidates dealt with this efficiently, mentioning class, poverty, nature and nurture to support points they were making, there was a useful decline in less successful candidates over-reliance on context and sweeping generalisations regarding the rich and poor.

Summary of key points

Characteristics of a good Section A response:

● Use the extract purposefully, highlighting key details that help focus on the question and provide useful AO2 comments. ● Use the extract as a springboard into a wider discussion of the text. ● Focus on well-chosen key events or scenes, significant characters/relationships to link to the question and wider themes. ● Have a sustained focus and direct textual references with good coverage of the text (referencing events spanning the beginning, middle and ending of the story). ● Clear planning and progression of the response, with development of ideas and supporting references, rather than assertions and general impressions.

Ways in which performance can be improved:

● Remind candidates of the bullet points built into the start of every question and use them to shape responses. ● Encourage candidates to be selective in their use of the extract to demonstrate their AO2 skills. There is no requirement on component 2 to analyse the extract in detail. Instead, use the extract as a springboard for a wider discussion, with a few key words or images explored that can then be broadened out to show knowledge and understanding of the whole text. ● Avoid ‘over analysis’ of vocabulary. ‘Mrs Lyons says Edward was a ‘tiny baby’. The adjective ‘tiny’ suggests her problems and life with her husband were ‘tiny’ ● Avoid repeatedly labelling or naming every word class. Be selective. Also, avoid forcing techniques and subject terminology into their responses to the extract – either incorrectly or very tenuously: ‘the use of a descending tricolon causes Ralph and Jack to seem much closer to each other’.

33 ● Avoid focus on analysis of sentence length, punctuation features or more nonfiction rhetorical devices, which again, can be an unproductive use of the extract. It also would be better to avoid unnecessary terms such as semantic fields or lexical sets and replace with simple reference to ‘words’ or ‘phrases’. ● Contextual details should only really be included in section a if relevant to the question and then still need to be closely tied to discussion of the characters, events and details. For example, Priestley’s intentions in writing An Inspector Calls still neede to be closely tied to discussion of the play. Too often, context is confused and very general (e.g., ‘during the 1960s, or the Industrial Revolution, women were seen as failures if they didn’t stay home and have babies’). These are not particularly helpful, relevant or accurate. ● Encourage pupils to learn key spellings such as character names and authors, as well as key words associated with each text. ● Proof-read responses to section a to eradicate simple errors such as capital letters or missing apostrophes and avoid combined words such as “alot” and the increasingly prevalent “eachother”. ● Responses must be legible.
c720u20-jun24-21-q:
Candidates responded well to the question that focussed on Scrooge and how his thoughts and feelings about Christmas change during the course of the novel. Most explored Scrooge's transformation effectively and how his views changed regarding Christmas. Inevitably, some candidates tried to crowbar the whole novel into their discussion in chronological order, whereas those candidates that used their planning time to select more judiciously, were inevitably rewarded with a higher mark as they were able to discuss their selections in more depth. However, the openness of the question allowed all approaches to be valid. In general, the most popular approach was tackling each stave in turn and tracking how Scrooge’s views on Christmas change with each supernatural visit. This allowed candidates to demonstrate secure knowledge of characters and the whole text. Less able candidates sometimes tended to consider Scrooge’s character at the start and at the end, with little reference to the middle of the novel and the events that actually changed Scrooge. However, the vast majority of candidates knew the text well, with numerous references to Scrooge as a ‘solitary child’, and the influence of Fezziwig, Belle, the Cratchits’ Christmas, Tiny Tim’s death and Scrooge’s own future death. In terms of using the extract, a range of approaches was seen. Some candidates chose to write about the extract first, however, given the extract’s position at the end of the novel, many candidates understandably chose to explore it at the end of their essays, having dealt with the events of the wider text as they unfold chronologically in the story. All approaches were valid. Better responses often explored AO2 by commenting on the pathetic fallacy of ‘golden sunlight’ in the extract and comparing the weather with the freezing “fog” at the start of the novel. The similes of, “light as a feather” and comparison to a baby were well discussed and often contrasted with other language points elsewhere in the wider text.

34 The question gave plenty of scope for the inclusion of context, which was assessed as AO3. The quality of discussion naturally varied significantly. There was much discussion of Malthusian theory and how it related to Scrooge’s views, and some discussion of Christmas traditionally being a time of family and giving. There was also consideration of Dickens’ purpose in writing the novella, and the ways in which Scrooge and Cratchit represented contemporary society. There were also many varied comments about Dickens’ own family experiences of poverty, debtors’ prisons and working in a blacking factory. Sometimes context was either ‘bolted on’ (i.e. provided as stand-alone paragraphs) or ‘implicit’ (i.e. not consciously included). Both these approaches are self-penalising. A Christmas Carol is easily the most popular of the Section B texts and continues to remain accessible to the complete ability range of candidates. The numerous film versions are no doubt a big reason for this, and while useful teaching tools, candidates should be cautioned against clear references to film versions that don’t appear in the text.
c720u20-jun24-22-q: Silas Marner continues to work well for a range of abilities. The question required candidates to focus on Eppie and her importance to the novel as a whole. All candidates seemed to be able to relate Eppie to Silas and the change and significance she played in his life. The extract worked well in allowing candidates to discuss stylistic features in terms of Eppie’s presentation as a replacement for Silas’s love for his gold as well as exploring Eliot’s rich evocative descriptions of nature in relation to Eppie. There was plenty here for candidates to explore such as, “new joy” and “seeking and loving sunshine” and most took full advantage. The majority of candidates focussed on Eppie's effect on Silas, but more able candidates brought in discussion of Godfrey Cass and Aaron Winthrop to discuss Eppie’s importance in the novel as a whole. In terms of AO3, centres had obviously prepared candidates well with regard to context with some good and varied discussion of the romantics, attitudes to women and children born out of wedlock, industrialisation and religion in relation to the novel.
c720u20-jun24-23-q:
The question asked candidates to consider some of the violent events in War of the Worlds and their importance to the novel as a whole.

Candidates largely used the extract well and often wrote about the atmosphere created by the first paragraph, the words and actions of the women and the terrible destructive power of the tripods, as well as their steadily increasing numbers and the narrator’s description of them.

Many candidates successfully commented on specific examples of violence in the novel and linked this to the ways the Martian invasion caused law and order to break down in the novel. Many candidates focused on the physical and environmental destruction caused by violent events in the novel, but many also successfully explored the effect that violent events had on the emotional and psychological wellbeing of some of the characters such as the narrator, the Curate and the Artilleryman.

35 Discussions of the theme were often linked well to AO3 points of context and Wells’ critical views on Victorian pillars of society such as the Church and the Military, as well as valid references to the survival of the fittest; Tasmania; the British Empire; and Imperialism all of which were often skilfully used.
c720u20-jun24-24-q:
Pride and Prejudice again proved to be relatively popular as a text studied across a large part of the ability range. Candidates responded well to the opportunities offered by the question, which called on candidates to consider the presentation of marriage in the novel.

Most responses were extremely well focussed and provided a wide range of specific support from the wider text (either paraphrased reference to events or direct supporting reference). Most candidates were able to place the extract precisely in the timeline of events and were able to discuss the conflict that Elizabeth’s engagement to Darcy created with Lady Catherine de Bourgh.

Many candidates relished the opportunity to discuss Elizabeth and Darcy’s changing views on marriage through their unconventional courtship. The most successful responses also referenced a range of other characters and the attitudes to marriage they reflected including Mr and Mrs Bennet, Charlotte Lucas and Mr. Collins, Jane and Bingley, and Wickham and Lydia.

The best answers were able to link discussion of the text to AO3 by discussing characters’ views of marriage within the wider frame of societal views and attitudes to women, marriage, status and class.

A minority of responses remained overly reliant on film adaptations of the novel and took a narrative approach which lacked depth and detail of direct evidence and quotations from the text.
c720u20-jun24-25-q:
Jane Eyre continues to be a relatively popular text once again, with a fair ability range amongst candidates. This open question focused on sympathy for Jane in the novel and this allowed the majority of candidates to provide assured, confident and evaluative discussion of the text.

The extract was taken from near the start of the novel, so it was understandable that the vast majority of the candidates used it as a starting point for their discussions. The extract allowed for perceptive discussion of AO2 features such as imperative language, dialogue, superlatives and questions and how these were used by Brontë to elicit sympathy for Jane.

A common approach for many candidates was to track through the text in terms of places Jane spent her life and reference the sympathy for the suffering she endured in these places. As a result, there was much appropriate discussion of Jane’s conflict with the Reeds, Mr Brocklehurst, Rochester and St John. Often, these discussions were detailed, thoughtful and perceptive. A significant number of responses sensibly featured detailed reference to the revelation of Bertha Mason’s existence, and this was often used as an opportunity to skilfully weave in AO3 references to gender, religion, economic status, social class and sensitive parallels between Jane and the real-life situation of Charlotte Brontë.

36 Overall, this was a very successful question for the candidates who studied the novel. However, an overemphasis on different critical interpretations of the text remains largely unhelpful. A number of candidates commented at length on rehearsed readings of the text in “bolted on” pseudo psychological interpretations of the “Red Room”, comparisons of the Reeds to Moses, or Gateshead to the “gates of heaven” at the expense of demonstrating detailed knowledge of the text.
c720u20-jun24-26-q:
The question focused on the ways Stevenson creates mystery at different points in the novel and worked well. All candidates were able to incorporate their knowledge of plot and characters and respond to the question in a variety of valid ways.

Most candidates were aided by the extract. Film versions seemed to be less prevalent this year, though were still occasionally present. Candidates engaged fully with the extract, discussion of which at times, also led to full coverage of the text and Jekyll/Hyde’s eventual death. The majority of responses referenced key aspects of the wider text e.g., Jekyll’s scientific experimentation or “heresies” and Hyde’s character. Candidates often widened the scope of their discussions to include the mystery of Hyde’s “troglodytic” appearance, “ape like fury” and “Satan’s signature”; the murder of Sir Danvers Carew and Lanyon’s death and the way these were revealed.

The top band responses widened their scope further with some nuanced and sensitive discussion of Utterson’s gradual discoveries. There was also some sensitive discussion of the way different points of view and first-person narratives, such as the accounts left by Dr Lanyon and Dr Jekyll, contributed to the theme of mystery in the text. Context was purposefully addressed by many candidates, especially those who commented on the central mystery of the “duality” of man and linked this to concepts of respectability, repression and reputation. Some candidates surprisingly did not mention Hyde which limited their responses significantly.

Summary of Key Points

Points to remember:

● The first key question for the examiner is: ‘Does the candidate know the text well?’ ● The second key question for the examiner is: ‘Has the candidate answered the question in a focused and sustained way?’ ● AO2 and AO3 are worth a third of the marks but are not expected to take up a third of the essay • responses must be legible.

Characteristics of good Section B essay responses:

● Clear and sustained focus on the question asked. ● Appropriate selection of short references to support the points made. ● Coverage of, and reference to, a range of relevant points across the wider text. ● Critical probing of inferences, implicit meanings and subtext as well as more surface ideas. ● Close analysis of how the language and writer’s techniques in the extract and wider text help to present the focus of the question. ● Clear appreciation of how contextual factors influence characters and themes. ● Suitable analytical style of writing.

37 Ways in which performance could be improved:

● Plan where coverage of the extract will be best placed in the essay. ● More detailed coverage of the extract and wider text, including the beginning, middle and end. ● More selection of detailed supporting references rather than general impressions. ● Avoid unfocused narrative and retelling of the story. ● More practice on exploring subtext and interpretation. ● Practise creating clear, cohesive arguments which address the question asked. ● More focused and integrated discussion of how contextual factors influence writers’ characters, themes and ideas. Avoid contextual ‘bolt-ons’. ● Careful adherence to the rubric requirements of the paper to ensure that candidates are only answering questions on the texts that they have studied. ● Avoid reference to plays and films when discussing prose texts. ● Practise and develop an analytical style of essay writing.
c720u20-jun24-31-q: The Newcomer was accessible to the vast majority of candidates. The relatively straightforward ideas and accessible style allowed nearly all candidates to identify and demonstrate understanding of at least some of the key ideas. Many were able to empathise with the animals and could passionately relate to the issue of the environmental impact of humans, often with a sense of guilt. More able candidates looked at the content in more detail, discussing the newcomer’s ability to bypass the “impassible dam” or to dig deeper than the animals dared, and the animals’ varying reactions to it. The “Newcomer” was considered to be variously amazing, foolish, powerful or dangerous, with some candidates suggesting that the animals observed and respected the laws and boundaries of nature whereas the newcomer was disrespectful and dismissive of them. Candidates talked about the unity between the animals, how they were passing on information to each other about the newcomer, and interacting with species they would not normally interact with. The fact that the news was “spreading fast” and had spread throughout the animal kingdom reinforced the idea that the newcomer was everywhere and that it was prolific. A small minority of the candidates failed to grasp the deliberate ambiguity in the poem and did not understand that the “Newcomer” was human, but they were often able to gain credit for exploring the idea that this was someone or something strange and unusual. However, most understood the central idea well and linked the evidence in the poem to man-made machinery, pollution, litter or climate change with great success. The animals’ reactions were often well discussed, with suggestions such as they were curious, confused, in admiration, and frightened. Many candidates were able to gain AO2 credit for discussion of the repetition at the beginning of the first four stanzas, and the regular pattern of these, contrasting with changes in the fifth and final stanza and the significance of this. Many suggested that the repetition of the first line, emphasised that the newcomer was everywhere in the animal kingdom. They also highlighted the repetition in the final stanza, and discussed the use of ‘and’ with varying degrees of success. The more successful responses considered how the repetition implied a continuous action, that the killing went on and on and on. There was some sensitive consideration of the change in tone between the first four stanzas and the final one. Some candidates talked about the childlike feel to the first four stanzas, and the contrasting and violent content of the final stanza. The personification of the animals was discussed, with candidates feeling that this enabled them to empathise more with the animals as it enabled the reader to see and understand the effects, we are having on the animal kingdom. There seemed to be fewer far-fetched interpretations of the poem, though some related the poem to being a newcomer themselves and suggested the poem was about starting at a new school and feeling excluded. Overall, this poem was very well received, and most candidates were able to produce relevant and considered responses to the text.
c720u20-jun24-32-q:
The pairing of The Newcomer by Brian Patten and The Fish Are All Sick by Anne Stevenson gave the candidates plenty to discuss in terms of comparison and worked well across the entire ability range. As the more challenging poem, candidates were generally less secure with the second poem compared to the first, but most were able to grasp the main key ideas of the poem. The second poem was felt by many to be more serious and more critical of humans. Most candidates understood the idea of something bad happening to the environment of the beach and the sea and identified this as caused by humans. The littered beach was often discussed, and the idea of the unknown attacker was interpreted as either humans or often a kind of oil spill. Better candidates engaged with the image of the ‘villages stranded’, and this was sometimes interpreted as villages that had been victim to coastal erosion, and the ‘pearls’ an indictment of human’s plundering of the natural world for the sake of aesthetics. Another discriminator tended to be discussion of the “big glass views and begonia beds” which were often interpreted as beautiful or out of place, with some candidates linking the glass views to building and construction, tourism or even humans putting wildlife into captivity. Effective responses compared the poems in a logical way, making clear links between the two texts. The tone of each poem was mentioned quite often, and many students expressed a preference for The Newcomer as it seemed lighter and more child friendly in their opinion. Many could pick out the harsher, blunter approach of Stevenson and also the differing focus of the whole animal kingdom in the first poem compared to sea life in the second. There was lots of discussion about the repetition in each poem, with more able candidates not just highlighting the use of this stylistic feature but exploring its effect and considering the writers’ intentions. More thoughtful responses explored the poets’ intentions and sense of ongoing doom for the environment and natural world. They highlighted this doom at the end of both poems by linking, “And it kills, and it kills, and it kills,” with “And closing its grip, and closing its grip.” Some candidates thought the second poem was more explicit and was clearly blaming humans for the negative impact on the environment, whilst the first poem was considered more subtle and less accusatory. Both had a similar effect on the reader of making them feel sad or guilty about the negative impact humans have on the environment. It was clear that the poems gave candidates the opportunity to reflect on environmental damage and the natural world and many did this in a mature way, with thought and consideration. Overall, candidates gave every impression of having enjoyed writing about the poems and levels of engagement were very high.

40 Summary of Key Points

Characteristics of good poetry responses:

● A thorough examination of the first poem in 3.1. ● A thorough examination of the second poem in 3.2, either as a discrete element or as part of the comparison. ● Recognition of the stated overview of the poems (found underneath the question on the paper). ● Clear comparison of ideas, mood and some reference to how the poets use language. ● Detailed selection and coverage from each poem with supporting comments exploring the meaning and effects of these selections.

Ways in which performance can be improved:

● Use the statement at the start of the question as a focus as it gives an overview of what the poems are about. ● Ensure that the first poem is adequately analysed in 3.1. ● Ensure that the second poem is adequately analysed in depth in 3.2. ● Practise commenting on a range of poems and poetic techniques, including imagery and figurative language. ● Avoid spotting and labelling techniques and patterns with no reference to meaning. ● Develop the use of supporting references to support understanding of subtext. ● Avoid ‘over reading’ of hidden meanings in the poems. ● Gain experience in reading poems where similar topics are handled differently by poets. ● Rehearse timings across the exam to ensure sufficient time is given to the poetry. ● Make sure a range of comparative points are made in 3.2. ● Responses must be legible.
c720u20-jun25-01-q:
The extract proved to be very accessible, with most candidates able to discuss how the scene fitted into the theme of conflict in the novel. Many candidates took the opportunity to comment on Golding's use of light imagery, the impending storm and its significance, and how the childish language emphasised the ages of the boys. Discussion of Simon and his tentative assertion that "maybe there is a beast" were given appropriate attention as were the contributions of Ralph and Piggy. The use of short bursts of dialogue were commented on by many to gain AO2 credit.

In the wider text, most candidates sensibly chose to focus on the growing conflict between Jack and Ralph in regard to their priorities and decision-making. This often widened and developed into discussion of conflicting attitudes and beliefs, settings and ideologies. The very best responses covered key events from the whole novel and included the ending, leading up to the final moments and what many perceived as conflict resolution.
c720u20-jun25-02-q:
It was very pleasing to see an uptake of this text by centres, with candidates providing engaged, knowledgeable responses. Most of these made extremely good use of the extract to write about Mama's hard-working ethic and her total commitment to looking after her family, often taking the opportunity to explore techniques used by Syal in the extract, such as listing, personification, alliteration and onomatopoeia and then commenting of the effect of these in presenting Mama's character. The very best explored the "swapping saris for M&S separates" quote as a springboard into the way Mama reflected the conflict and integration of cultures in the novel.

21 In terms of the wider text, many candidates compared the parenting styles of Meena’s mother with Anita’s mother, Deirdre, and there was a lot of mature discussion on cultural expectations. The poignancy of Mama’s sense of alienation was nicely juxtaposed with her willingness to see the best in British life and wry humour in the face of its shortcomings. The effect of Sunil’s arrival on both mother and daughter was often sensitively handled as was Nanima’s contribution.
c720u20-jun25-03-q:
This was the first year of examination for this text and it proved very successful, working well for the full range of candidates across the entire ability range. The question, on the theme of growing up in the novel, provided candidates with an open opportunity to discuss characters, events and their presentation in the novel.

Many candidates sensibly used the extract as a starting point for their exploration of the theme. There was widespread recognition of the turning point in Dante's attitudes towards Emma, with much discussion of the simile likening Emma to a "fence which needed to be knocked down". This often led on to Dante's use of pronouns when describing Emma, turning from 'it' to 'her' as an example of how he matures.

Whilst many candidates understandably focussed on Dante and his attitudes and relationship with Emma, many more widened out the focus to include other characters like Adam, Emma herself, Josh and even Tyler. There was much relevant discussion on toxic masculinity, and it seems like the text resonated with candidates in this respect.
c720u20-jun25-04-q:
The question provided candidates with an open opportunity to discuss shock and horror in the novel. Many candidates took advantage of this to analyse key moments, characters and settings. Most candidates used the extract effectively to analyse Hill’s use of imagery in describing the way horror was built, with frequent references to pathetic fallacy (e.g. the way fog builds isolation), Hill's use of aural imagery to create a sense of disorientation, and the use of a child to convey horror at their distress and loss.

Many candidates went on to discuss the shock of the woman in black’s appearance at Alice Drablow’s funeral, often using last year's extract to good effect. Other well-chosen moments included discussion of Arthur Kipps' experiences and discoveries at Eel Marsh House and the deaths of Stella and Joseph at the end of the novel.

Film references continue to be a particular issue for a significant minority of candidates on this text, especially as they often deviate dramatically from the events of the novel. More selective use of the film version as a teaching aid is advisable.
c720u20-jun25-05-q:
Mrs Winterson, and her changing relationship with Jeanette, is central to the novel and the vast majority of candidates engaged well with the question. The extract provided a rich opportunity to discuss Mrs Winterson’s uncompromising character. Those that used the extract well often noted Winterson’s presentation of Mrs Winterson's hypocrisy, e.g. "She said he was a devil, but she still took the mince." Candidates also frequently mentioned the character's snobbery, e.g. “keeping her 'H' as best she could”. Many responses also explored the difficult relationship with Jeanette, noting the final line of the extract, "I hated her." Often this was used this as a springboard into the wider novel, including discussion of Jeanette's hospital stay and her 'exorcism'. Many were also able to comment on the partial reconciliation between Jeanette and Mrs Winterson at the end of the novel.

It was also pleasing to note the recognition of the humour that the character provides in the extract and the wider novel. Similarly, the frequent purposeful references to the text's mythic elements, with comments on the allegorical nature of these elements, were also signifiers of candidates achieving marks in the higher bands.
c720u20-jun25-06-q:
The question on Christopher's father, Ed, was very successful in providing the opportunity for some thoughtful, perceptive and heartfelt responses from candidates. It enabled them to evaluate whether Ed can be forgiven for hitting Christopher. The best responses discussed Ed’s role in Christopher’s life, often in comparison to Judy, and the challenges involved in raising a child with autism.

Many candidates commented successfully on the extract, in particular the mocking tone of, “Come on, you're the memory man…”, the repeated questioning of Christopher by Ed, e.g. "What am I going to do with you, Christopher?". There was often some interesting discussion about the use of stage directions in the extract and the shocking and impactful moment when, "Ed hits the side of Christopher’s head."

Candidates who study this play really seem to engage and connect with it, and answers don’t tend to contain the ‘bolted on’ context (not assessed) that some of the other text choices in Section A seem to attract. However, there were a significant number of weaker responses where candidates either copied the extract completely, or copied large chunks of the extract without making any comment.
c720u20-jun25-07-q:
This was the first year that this text had been examined and it proved very successful, working well for the full range of candidates across the ability range. The question, on the character of Enid, provided candidates with an opportunity to discuss the character's background, family relationships and her connection to the play's themes and provided a good basis for some very confident and sensitive responses. Many candidates commented on key moments such as the subdued nature of the character as detailed in the opening stage directions, and the rare opening up to Viv about her previous life in the Caribbean.

In the wider text, many candidates discussed Enid’s reaction to Del’s pregnancy and the way she reacts to and treats Viv, particularly in respect to her education. Some candidates also discussed the presentation of Enid in terms of her determination to have a better life and how house-proud this has made her. Her often-difficult relationship with her children was a rich seam of discussion with many discussing the end of the text and the partial reconciliation between Enid and Del.
c720u20-jun25-08-q:
An Inspector Calls continues to remain the most popular of the Section A texts by a considerable margin. The play proved once again to be engaging and accessible to the complete ability range of candidates who were able to discuss Gerald Croft and his importance to the play as a whole. The vast majority were able to engage with the extract and demonstrate secure knowledge of the wider text.

A range of valid approaches was used. Some candidates chose to track Gerald’s role chronologically from the beginning, while others used the extract as a springboard into a discussion of his relationships with Sheila and Daisy. The extract worked well in enabling candidates to reflect on Gerald and Sheila's relationship and the revelation of his affair with Daisy Renton. Sheila's sarcastic use of the phrase "fairy prince" was thoughtfully explored by some candidates. In terms of his relationship with Daisy Renton, some candidates argued that he was kind to her, giving Daisy money to live on when he leaves her, and was then saddened by her death; others argued that he abused Daisy in much the same way as Alderman Meggarty, and had shown no regret about his actions, only giving her a small amount of money when he leaves. There were also responses that promoted a mix of these interpretations. All responses were taken openly and rewarded on merit.

Successful responses tended to focus on the description of Gerald in the opening stage directions which describe Gerald as an "easy well-bred young man-about-town". Many interpreted "bred" (often misspelled as "bread") having animalistic connotations and implying that he had been trained to act a particular way in his class. The phrase "man-about-town" was often interpreted as proof of his familiarity with the Palace Bar. Other frequent mentions were given to Gerald's interactions with Mr Birling over dinner, and his role and reaction to the final revelation that the Inspector is not real at the end of the play. The engagement ring attracted some attention, not only as a symbol of Gerald’s control over Sheila, because he chose it for her, but as a symbol of the cyclical nature of the play. The best responses were able to evaluate Gerald's position between the younger and older generations and many candidates made the point that, as Gerald is not in the room for the Inspector’s “fire and blood and anguish” speech, he doesn’t fully appreciate the lesson he has to learn. Although context is not rewarded in Section A of this component, it understandably has an integral part to play in the teaching of this text. The majority of candidates were at least aware of the issues of class, Capitalism versus Socialism, and the patriarchal society at the time the play is set.

Weaker responses sometimes confused the characters of Eric and Gerald, mixing up events from both characters' involvement with Eva Smith, however these were relatively rare. Some candidates tried to crowbar in information on other characters, e.g. Mr Birling’s attitudes to business and his erroneous opinions, sometimes linked to Gerald with just a short sentence. References to Gerald’s 'toxic masculinity’ were abundant and often not totally secure in the context of the character.

AO4 is assessed in this question. As always, there were many variations in the spelling of key names, e.g. Priestley, Birling and Sheila. There were also many instances of not using capital letters for proper nouns.
c720u20-jun25-09-q:
Responses to this text continue to be, on the whole, of a very high standard. This seems to be a text that is well chosen by centres who know their candidates’ ability to respond sensitively to its humour, themes and messages about the human condition. These candidates were well prepared to discuss Irwin’s character in the extract and wider play.

24 Candidates wrote of Irwin’s meretricious nature; his significance in the boys’ development, both educationally and in growing up; his significance as a representative of the new education system; and his sexual predilections. The extract was often thoroughly explored with perceptive understanding of Irwin's self-serving intentions beneath the guise he employs of improving the boys’ educational prospects. As ever, not all answers got to talk about the end of the play, but a number did make pertinent comments on Bennett’s structure through talking about the prolepsis and the boys’ slow desertion of Hector. Comparison with Hector and educational methods was pertinent but occasionally some candidates focussed more on Hector and occasionally lost focus on Irwin.

Film references were sometimes an issue for a small minority of candidates on this text, who commented on things that don’t happen in the play. Selective use of the film version as a teaching aid is advisable.
c720u20-jun25-10-q:
The question worked extremely well across the full range of abilities. The vast majority of candidates had a very good knowledge of Mrs Lyons' character and the play as a whole. A large number of candidates tracked through Mrs Lyons' chronological appearances in the play and this approach often led to well-structured essays. These candidates often included the extract early in their response, in keeping with its placing in the early part of the play. Weaker students often relied on the extract, making only generalised references to the wider play, or occasionally no wider detail at all.

Many thoughtful responses explored how Mrs Lyons manipulates Mrs Johnstone, preying on her superstitious beliefs when inventing the superstition about the twins. Many used the quotation, "You will kill them," to express Mrs Lyons’ desperation. Again, stronger candidates analysed how the stage directions highlighted Mrs Lyons’ anger, frustration and power over Mrs Johnstone, e.g. "picks up the money and thrusts it...". Many candidates discussed the theme of the inequality between social classes using details from the extract such as, "It’s a lot of money..." to explore the power imbalance between the two characters.

Generally, wider references to Mrs Lyons were plentiful, with many candidates tracking her character's mental deterioration over the course of the play, culminating in her attack on Mrs Johnstone. Some made a case for Mrs Lyons being a lonely and desperate woman, with her slapping of Edward often seen as an instinctive action which proved her villainy. Pleasingly, many candidates dealt with the end of the play and Mrs Lyons' contribution to the plot and ending of the play. Context is not explicitly rewarded in Section A but some stronger candidates dealt with this efficiently, mentioning class, poverty, and nature versus nurture to support points they were making about Mrs Lyons. There was another useful decline in less successful candidates' over-reliance on context and sweeping generalisations regarding the rich and poor. In terms of AO4, missing capitalisation of the play and the characters’ names was also frequent. As always, there were many variations of the spellings of "Johnstone" and "Russell".

25 Summary of key points

Characteristics of a good Section A response: • Using the extract purposefully, highlighting key details that help focus on the question and provide useful AO2 comments. • Using the extract as a springboard into a wider discussion of the text. • Focus on well-chosen key events or scenes, significant characters/relationships to link to the question and wider themes. • A sustained focus and direct textual references with good coverage of the text (referencing events spanning the beginning, middle and ending of the story). • Clear planning and progression of the response, with development of ideas and supporting references, rather than assertions and general impressions. • Close analysis of how the language, writer’s techniques in the extract and wider text help to present the focus of the question. • A suitably analytical style of writing.

Ways in which performance can be improved: • Candidates should use the bullet points built into the start of every question and use them to shape responses. • Candidates should be more selective in their use of the extract to demonstrate their AO2 skills. There is no requirement on Component 2 to analyse the extract in detail. Instead, use the extract as a springboard for a wider discussion, with a few key words or images explored that can then be broadened out to show knowledge and understanding of the whole text. • Avoid ‘over analysis’ of vocabulary, e.g. ‘Gerald and Sheila have an engagement party. The adjective 'engagement’ suggests they are getting married.' • Avoid repeatedly labelling or naming every word class. Be selective. Also, avoid forcing techniques and subject terminology into their responses to the extract – either incorrectly or very tenuously: ‘The use of a descending tricolon causes conflict between the boys’. • Avoid overly focussing on on analysis of sentence length, punctuation features or more nonfiction rhetorical devices, which again, can be an unproductive use of the extract. It also would be better to avoid unnecessary terms such as semantic fields or lexical sets and replace with simple reference to ‘words’ or ‘phrases’. • Plans containing points to cover and some key words are helpful and can be practised as part of examination preparation. However, full pages of quotes written down before the question often lead to shorter responses and should be discouraged. • Contextual details should only really be included in Section A if relevant to the question and then still need to be closely tied to discussion of the characters, events and details. For example, Priestley’s intentions in writing An Inspector Calls but still needed to be closely tied to discussion of the play. Too often, context is confused and very general (e.g. ‘The Industrial Revolution of the 1980s, or 'in the 1960s all women stayed at home having babies and were housewives’). These are not particularly helpful, relevant or accurate. • Encourage pupils to learn key spellings such as character names and authors, as well as key words associated with each text and so likely to be employed. • Proof-read responses to eradicate simple errors such as capital letters or missing apostrophes and avoid combined words such as “alot” and the increasingly prevalent “eachother”. • Avoid reference to plays and films when discussing prose texts. • Responses must be legible.
c720u20-jun25-21-q:
The question asked candidates to write about Scrooge and the way he is presented at different points in the novella using an extract where Scrooge visits the neglected grave shown to him by the final spirit. This proved to be a very accessible and engaging question that allowed candidates across the entire ability range to fully explore Dickens’ presentation of Scrooge in detail. The straightforward nature of the question enabled candidates to fully demonstrate their knowledge of the text and central character confidently and structure their ideas with ease. Most responses demonstrated a clear awareness of how Scrooge is depicted at various stages of the novella, with the contrast between the extract and his earlier appearances used effectively to track Dickens’ characterisation. Less successful answers often relied heavily on the extract or on a small set of overused quotations or offered generalised assertions about Scrooge’s character. There was also occasional confusion about key events or characters—for example, misidentifying which ghost reveals which vision, or conflating Fred and Bob Cratchit.

Many candidates structured their answers chronologically, beginning with the opening description of Scrooge as “hard and sharp as flint” and “solitary as an oyster”, and tracing how Dickens gradually reshapes his portrayal through key episodes such as the visits from the three spirits. Many candidates tracked the presentation of Scrooge chronologically, linking the extract’s fear and desperation with his earlier selfishness and eventual redemption. The best responses provided a detailed exploration of the extract, particularly the language of pleading and fear ("clutching at its robe", “trembling”, “I will honour Christmas in my heart”), and tied this into broader themes of redemption, social responsibility, and moral awakening. Other approaches began with the extract and then explored earlier depictions retrospectively. Both approaches worked well, although some weaker responses spent too long on narrative summary and struggled to develop analysis of character presentation.

The most successful responses examined how Dickens uses language, structure and symbolism to shape Scrooge’s portrayal at different points. In many responses candidates considered how the similes used early on present Scrooge as emotionally closed and disconnected from society, while later scenes—such as his reaction to Tiny Tim’s death or his pleas in the graveyard—highlight vulnerability and emotional growth. There was often perceptive comment on Dickens’ technique, such as the use of pathetic fallacy to mirror Scrooge’s emotional state, or the way the extract conveyed fear, desperation and transformation.

Contextual understanding was often well integrated. Many responses frequently referenced Dickens’ message about social responsibility, Christian morality, and attitudes towards poverty, with many citing Malthusian economics and Dickens’ own background. There was also reference to Dickens’ broader purpose in writing the novella, with the character of Scrooge used to challenge societal neglect of the poor and promote compassion and generosity. The best responses embedded this context naturally, enhancing their interpretation of Dickens’ presentation of Scrooge at different stages. Less successful answers often skipped over the middle of the novella or bolted on context in isolated paragraphs, rather than integrating it meaningfully.

27 This question enabled most candidates to demonstrate sound knowledge of the text. Less confident responses were able to comment on Dickens’ presentation of Scrooge as cold and miserly at the start, and more emotional and generous later. Stronger responses went further, analysing the how and why of these shifts in presentation, and offering thoughtful interpretations of Dickens’ methods and messages. Overall, this was a well-received and productive question that elicited engaged and often thoughtful responses.
c720u20-jun25-22-q:
The question asked candidates to write about Silas and the way he is presented as important to the novel and produced some very confident, assured responses. Candidates engaged confidently with the presentation of Silas at different points in the novel, often demonstrating assured textual knowledge and perceptive interpretation.

Most responses were well-structured, typically beginning with Lantern Yard and moving through key developments in Raveloe. The extract was used effectively to link earlier and later depictions of Silas, allowing candidates to track Eliot’s presentation of the character with clarity. Higher-level responses explored Eliot’s language and imagery with precision, discussing recurring motifs of weaving, light, and fire, and showed sensitivity to shifts in narrative tone and perspective.

Context was generally well handled. Many candidates demonstrated a sound grasp of relevant social and historical ideas. The most successful responses integrated context meaningfully to illuminate Eliot’s intentions.

Overall, responses were consistently strong, with a significant number achieving the highest bands. Candidates showed genuine engagement with the character and responded with insight and maturity.
c720u20-jun25-23-q:
Candidates were asked to explore the narrator's importance to the novel. The extract described his emotional and physical exhaustion following a Martian attack. Responses generally demonstrated good understanding of the narrator’s psychological state, vulnerability, and role as an observer.

Most candidates linked this extract with key moments of terror and philosophical reflection in the wider novel, such as his encounters with the curate and artilleryman. Many discussed how the first-person narrative deepens reader engagement with the themes of chaos, survival, and imperial decline.
