Contextual references to Darwinism, colonialism, and Wells’ criticism of Victorian institutions were often included and well-developed. Less confident responses tended to focus on summarising events rather than analysing the narrator’s role and significance.
c720u20-jun25-24-q:
The question required candidates to explore Mr Darcy and his importance to the novel. The extract presented Darcy’s self-reflection and personal growth, and many candidates used this effectively to discuss how Darcy changes throughout the novel.

Strong responses focused on the language of remorse and growth (“selfish being,” “taught me a lesson”), and linked it to his developing relationship with Elizabeth. There was also apt discussion of Darcy’s role in upholding and challenging social norms.

28 Responses included discussion of gender, class, and marriage expectations in Regency England, with confident candidates integrating these points smoothly into their analysis. Weaker responses often defaulted to general plot retelling or overly relied on film versions.
c720u20-jun25-25-q:
This open question on Mr Rochester and his importance to the novel yielded a wide range of responses. The extract allowed candidates to analyse Rochester’s possessiveness, desperation, and conflicted emotions, especially regarding his proposal to Jane after revelations regarding Bertha Mason.

The most successful responses engaged closely with Rochester’s romantic and moral complexity, referencing key episodes like the fire rescue, the wedding interruption, and the reunion at Ferndean. These answers often explored Brontë’s presentation of power dynamics and emotional intensity. Evaluative commentary on Rochester’s relationship with Jane was often well-developed.

Contextual references to Victorian patriarchy, religious morality, and Brontë’s own experiences were often strong. Less successful responses struggled to fully address Rochester’s flaws or the moral implications of his actions.
c720u20-jun25-26-q:
The question focused on Mr Hyde and his importance to the novel. The extract provided a rich basis for discussing the theme of duality, with Jekyll’s reflections on Hyde’s “full deformity” and the battle for dominance between them.

Most candidates responded well, with even less secure answers able to discuss key events. “Trampled calmly” and “ape-like fury” were frequently cited, though stronger responses moved beyond these to analyse a wider range of evidence and Hyde’s symbolic role. Stronger candidates offered perceptive analysis of the language (“slime of the pit,” “co-heir to death”) and how Hyde represents repressed desires or the darker side of human nature. Many made links to key episodes such as the trampling of the girl and the murder of Carew. A number of responses showed confusion around the phrase 'temporary suicide' and the novel’s conclusion, however, most candidates showed clear understanding of Hyde’s significance and made strong use of the extract and wider text to support their views.

Context was generally well integrated. Candidates often included discussion of Victorian anxieties around scientific experimentation, morality, secrecy, and respectability. Many candidates provided thoughtful commentary on the dual nature of the gentleman and the role of setting. Some candidates continue to discuss the influence of Freudian theory which was often overapplied and unhelpful. Some candidates did not fully address Hyde, limiting the depth of their response.

29 Summary of Key Points

Points to remember:

• The first key question for the examiner is: ‘Does the candidate know the text well?’ • The second key question for the examiner is: ‘Has the candidate answered the question in a focused and sustained way?’ • AO2 and AO3 are worth a third of the marks but are not expected to take up a third of the essay. • Responses must be legible. Candidates who struggle with their handwriting can use word processors.

Characteristics of good Section B essay responses:

• A clear and sustained focus on the question asked. • Using the extract at a relevant point of the essay. • An appropriate selection of short references to support points made. • Coverage of, and reference to, a range of relevant points across the wider text. • Critical probing of inferences, implicit meanings and subtext as well as more surface ideas. • Close analysis of how the language, writer’s techniques in the extract and wider text help to present the focus of the question. • Clear appreciation of how contextual factors influence characters and themes. • A suitably formal analytical style of writing.

Ways in which performance could be improved:

• Practise of, and development of, an analytical style of essay writing. • Plan where coverage of the extract will be best placed in the essay. • More detailed coverage of the extract and wider text, including the beginning, middle and end. • More selection of detailed supporting direct references. • Avoid unfocused narrative and retelling of the story. • More practice on exploring subtext and interpretations. • Practise creating clear, cohesive arguments which address the question asked. • More focused and integrated discussion of how contextual factors influence writers’ characters, themes and ideas. Avoid contextual ‘bolt-ons’. • Careful adherence to the rubric requirements of the paper to ensure that candidates are only answering questions on the texts that they have studied. • Avoid reference to plays and films when discussing prose texts.
c720u20-jun25-31-q:
This question was accessible to all candidates, with the poem’s vivid imagery and extended metaphor of Autumn as a thief provoking engaged, thoughtful personal responses. Most candidates discussed the extended metaphor of theft, the role of the wind, and the changing mood of the poem.

Stronger responses analysed how Bold creates mood using personification, such as “the wind is his accomplice” and “glows red with a quiet rage”. These answers addressed both structure and tone shifts, recognising how the poem’s seemingly playful opening becomes more ominous.

Weaker responses tended to paraphrase the content or feature-spot, but engagement was generally high.
c720u20-jun25-32-q:
The comparative question invited candidates to explore similarities and differences between the two seasonal poems. Most understood that both poems reflected on seasonal change, decay, and the passage of time, though Patricia Beer’s poem was often seen as more sombre.

Stronger responses compared Bold’s vivid image of autumn as a thief “grabbing the green stuff” with Beer’s portrayal of winter’s slow, creeping presence through the “rolling shadow”. Many candidates also compared the sense of sudden loss and chaos in the poem Autumn in contrast to the slower, steady, inevitable change of seasons in Frost on the Shortest Day.

Most candidates engaged well with Autumn’s depiction as an “experienced robber,” appreciating the poem’s humour and use of colour imagery. Many explored the sense of loss and nature’s limited control over seasonal change, especially through the image of the sky “glowing red with a quiet rage.”

31 ‘Frost on the Shortest Day’ posed more challenges, though most candidates identified its key events. Stronger responses examined the imagery of “heavy frost” and the metaphorical suggestion of disease, as well as the resistance implied by the “sheep who hold their ground.” The sun’s inability to “lick” the frost and the inevitability of darkness were also thoughtfully discussed. A small number of candidates struggled with the more abstract elements of Beer’s poem but were still able to comment on key aspects of its content, imagery, and tone.

Comparisons frequently focused on the different seasons and the contrasting use of colour, particularly the recurring green. Candidates noted nature’s powerlessness and the disruptive effects of weather, as well as broader themes of time passing. While some responses interpreted the poems in terms of death or ageing, these alternative readings often overlooked the explicit instruction in the question that both poems are about different times of the year; candidates are advised to anchor their interpretations within the thematic focus provided.

Summary of Key Points

Characteristics of good poetry responses:

• A thorough examination of the first poem in 3.1. • A thorough examination of the second poem in 3.2, either as a discrete element or as part of the comparison. • Recognition of the stated overview of the poems (found underneath the question on the paper). • Clear comparison of ideas, mood and some reference to how the poets use language. • Detailed selection and coverage from each poem with supporting comments exploring the meaning and effects of these selections.

Ways in which performance can be improved:

• Use the statement at the start of the question as a focus as it gives an overview of what the poems are about. • Ensure that the first poem is adequately analysed in 3.1. • Ensure that the second poem is adequately analysed in depth in 3.2 • Practise commenting on a range of poems and the effects of poetic techniques, including imagery and figurative language. • Avoid spotting and labelling techniques and patterns with no reference to meaning. • Develop the use of supporting references to support understanding of subtext. • Avoid ‘over reading’ of hidden meanings in the poems. • Rehearse timings across the exam to ensure sufficient time is given to the poetry. • Make sure a range of comparative points are made in 3.2. • Responses must be legible.
c720u20-nov20-01-q:
The extract proved to be accessible and a good opportunity to discuss the character of Ralph. Many candidates used it as a springboard into a discussion of how Ralph’s position amongst the boys had deteriorated by this point, before showing how he had got to this situation through the previous events in the novel. Some took a more linear approach, tracking Ralph’s character throughout the novel and then weaving in the extract towards the end of their response. A significant weaker minority, however, did not use the extract in great detail and this invariably limited these candidates’ success in terms of AO2. These candidates tended not to reference the end of the book at all and were sometimes confused over the order and details of events.

Some candidates chose to focus on the relationship between Ralph and Jack in the course of their responses. Whilst there was often a lot to credit in this approach, a minority of candidates lost focus on the question and drifted into discussion of Jack. To a lesser extent, the same was true of those candidates who also approached the question through Ralph’s relationship with Piggy, though these tended to have a stronger focus on Ralph. The most able candidates linked Ralph’s fall from power to broader ideas of the breakdown of civilisation in the text.

This passage evoked some perceptive close reading, with most candidates exploring the physically broken Ralph through the repetition in the extract of the word “limped”. The character’s seeming lack of hope at this point was referenced, especially “No fire; no smoke; no rescue”. and better candidates discussed his fear through the selection of “terror”, “flesh crept” and “shivered”.
c720u20-nov20-02-q:
In a unique series, given the exceptional context of 2020, the vast majority of candidates studied An Inspector Calls. A small minority studied Lord of the Flies and Blood Brothers.

Rubric Infringements

There were a number of rubric infringements where responses were only based on the extracts set and did not reflect study of those texts. This is to be expected on an untiered paper, and was more evident in Section A, where there were far more rubric infringement responses (especially on questions 01-05). While marks can be awarded for sensible comments made from tracking the extract, the responses are obviously only limited to that section of the text and cannot demonstrate any wider textual knowledge, leaving them within Band 1 or low in Band 2 at best. Understandably, even the most well-prepared candidates can make this error under the extreme pressure of GCSE exams, and perhaps the context of reduced teaching and preparation time before this series added further to these errors.

The Paper

The source-based essay format was again successful in offering support in the closed-book, untiered exam. The questions worked across all texts for all abilities. There were a range of character, relationship and theme questions on texts.

Candidates generally responded well to the questions set. On the whole, candidates were able to demonstrate good understanding of the main events, characters and themes of the texts. Some candidates did not always comment on the ending of texts. This may have been a consequence of interrupted or reduced teaching time. Responses, overall, tended to show knowledge and understanding of texts in a narrative, rather than selective or evaluative, way.

Candidates took different approaches in responding to questions: some used the extract as a starting point for their essay, some took a more integrated approach by making links to the extract across the whole text. All approaches were valid. Although some candidates sensibly used the extracts as a means to demonstrate analysis of AO2 skills, many did not. As a result, the overall analysis of AO2 was less successful.

Timing Issues

It is still clear that some candidates spend significantly longer on the Section A text than their 19th Century Prose – which has a knock-on effect for their poetry responses too. Again, the reduction in teaching and preparation time may have meant that many candidates lost out on opportunities to rehearse answering on their set texts within 45 minutes and consequently may have been less familiar with the overall paper structure than in previous series.

AO4 – Spelling, punctuation, vocabulary and sentence structure accuracy

As reported last year, common errors include misspelling of character and author names with numerous variations of Priestley, Russell, Sheila, Johnstone etc. Run on sentences, or comma splicing also affected AO4 marks across the ability range. Similarly, missed capital letters and apostrophe misuse could be addressed when preparing pupils for Section A. Informal expression and illegibility also caused problems for even the most able candidates and is self-penalising.

Comments on individual questions/sections

c720u20-nov20-08-q:
The question’s focus, on the character of the Inspector, worked well and led to many focused and engaged responses. The question enabled more able students to comment in detail on the breadth of the play while less able candidates demonstrated a straightforward knowledge of events and related these to the Inspector’s investigation of Eva Smith’s death.

Candidates often started with a focus on the Inspector’s investigative methods in the extract and his immediate conflict with Mr Birling, before broadening out to take a systematic and structured, character-by-character approach to the question. In terms of AO2, the extract gave students the opportunity to provide a close analysis of the language. Discussion of stage directions was generally handled well and selection of “massiveness”, “looking hard at the person he is addressing”, and “cutting through” were all commonly selected and discussed well. Many candidates went on to make references to stage directions in other parts of the play, including Priestley’s suggestions about the lighting of the set changing on the Inspector’s arrival.

The structure of the play was well referenced, with a frequent analysis of significant moments and turning points, including the dramatic irony in the timing of the spotting by weaker candidates, which led to less successful responses.

The revelation at the end of the play, with the realisation that the Inspector was fake, was well referenced and discussed. At the lower end, this was handled in a very straightforward way, often with lengthy discussion on the supernatural nature of the Inspector, linked to the significance of Goole as his name. While valid, some of these would have benefited from further development.

More able candidates were able to discuss how the Inspector catalysed change in the younger generation and some stronger responses focussed on how the characters, within the drama, conveyed wider societal implications.

Priestley’s characterisation of the Inspector was also discussed as a means to demonstrate the conflict between capitalism and socialism in the play. Often, this was linked to discussion on how the Inspector was the ‘mouthpiece’ for Priestley’s own voice, including his clear views on class structure and the moral teachings he wished to impart to the audience.

As well as the extract, key speeches of the Inspector were often used to gain AO2 credit, most popularly and sensibly, his ‘fire, blood and anguish’ speech. Very astute candidates noted the Inspector’s use of “we” in this speech, and how he included himself in the sense of responsibility and blame. These responses demonstrated the ability to move from the specific to the general, which is a feature of top band responses.

The weaker candidates relied heavily or solely on the extract, often providing a focused analysis of details from the extract without addressing the wider text. Those that moved beyond the extract focused on a limited number of characters or events, or simply tended to list how the Inspector exposed the characters in terms of what they had done to Eva/Daisy without much development or explicit reference to the character of the Inspector. Lower band answers also tended to bolt on discussion of Priestley’s intentions in writing the play without linking to characters and events.

As with all Section A responses, there were up to five marks awarded for candidates’ use of vocabulary, spelling, punctuation and grammar. In terms of spelling, “Priestley”, “Birling”, “responsibility” and “Sheila” were often prone to errors. Missing capital letters for character names (including the Inspector) was a fairly common feature. Additionally, many candidates struggle to use the possessive apostrophe correctly.

c720u20-nov20-10-q:
A small number of candidates answered the question set on this text. The question worked well across a range of abilities in the responses seen.

The extract worked well as less able candidates were able to use it as a starting point to discuss Mickey and Linda. More able candidates commented on Linda’s manipulation of the situation, her attempts to make Mickey jealous and Mickey’s shyness and insecurities. Some candidates responded with limited discussion of Mickey and Linda’s relationship focusing only on them as children.

More able candidates tracked the relationship between Linda and Mickey from childhood, through childhood, adolescence, into adulthood and to the end of the play. These responses tended to use a range of approaches, some focused on Linda and Mickey in turn before bringing ideas together e.g. their role in childhood games, their behaviour at school and the relationship that then developed between them post-extract. The majority of responses were able to discuss the relationship between the characters in some detail. The most successful responses tracked through the play fully and thoroughly including details of the breakdown of Mickey and Linda’s relationship and Mickey’s death. At the highest level, candidates were able to evaluate the impact of the breakdown of Mickey and Linda’s relationship and its contribution to the tragic ending of the play.

Summary of key points

Characteristics of a good Section A response:

• Extract is used purposefully, highlighting key details that help focus on the question and provide AO2 comments • The extract is used as a springboard into a wider discussion of the text • A focus on well-chosen key events, scenes, characters and relationships to link to the question • Sustained focus • Direct textual references with good coverage of the text (referencing events spanning the beginning, middle and ending of the story) • Clear planning and progression in the response, with well-structured ideas

Ways in which performance can be improved:

• Use the extract purposefully, highlighting key details that help focus on the question and provide useful AO2 comments • Use the extract as a springboard into a wider discussion of the text • Focus on and select key events, scenes, characters and relationships that link to the question • Avoid narrative retelling of plot • Have good coverage of the text, referencing events spanning the full range, including the end of the story • Have a clear plan and progression in the response, with separate and logical ideas and focus • Include supporting references rather than just making general impressions and assertions • Remind candidates of the bullet points built into the start of every question and use them to shape responses • Avoid repeatedly labelling or naming every word class • Avoid forcing techniques and subject terminology into their responses to the extract – either incorrectly or very tenuously • Contextual details should only really be included in Section A if relevant to the question and then still need to be closely tied to discussion of the characters, events and details. For example, Priestley’s intentions in writing An Inspector Calls were central to this year's task but still needed to be closely tied to discussion of the play. • Learn key spellings such as character names and authors, as well as key words associated with each text and so likely to be employed

• Careful adherence to the rubric requirements of the paper to ensure that candidates are only answering questions on the texts that they have studied • Leave time to proofread responses to Section A to eradicate simple errors such as capital letters or missing apostrophes and avoid combined words such as “alot” and “eachother”
c720u20-nov20-21-q:
The question focused on how and why Scrooge changes from someone who wishes “to be left alone” in Stave One to his transformation at the end of the novel. The question called on candidates to select key events that cause this change in Scrooge’s character and comment on how Dickens presents them in the story.

The open nature of the question gave candidates of all abilities something to discuss and allowed candidates free rein to select the events they considered key in changing Scrooge’s attitudes. Invariably, some weaker candidates merely retold the story, though most had some focus on the question. Lots of candidates tracked confidently through the novel, selecting key moments such as the visitation of Marley’s Ghost; Scrooge witnessing his earlier break up with Belle; his growing concern for Tiny Tim; and witnessing his own death.

The extract was commonly used as a starting point to candidates’ essays, coming as it did from relatively early in the novel. Most were able to comment on how Scrooge “wept” to see his younger self. There was mixed understanding of the significance of Ali Baba in the extract, with many failing to grasp the imaginary nature of his presence. Nearly all, however, were able to comment on the range of emotion Scrooge demonstrated in witnessing him and link this to the question. A discriminator tended to be whether candidates got to the end of the extract and explained Scrooge’s regret for his earlier treatment of the carol singer at his door in Stave One.

Many candidates discussed with engagement and evaluation the ways in which Scrooge’s views were typical of some in Victorian society. Dickens’ intention in writing the book as a catalyst for change was well discussed, as was how the Cratchit family (and Tiny Tim in particular) acted as a key reason for Scrooge’s changing attitudes. It was pleasing to see a number of references to Ignorance and Want and, at the top, engaged discussion of the symbolism of these characters. Selection such as this allowed many candidates to discuss AO3 purposely and explore the divide between the rich and the poor in Victorian Britain.

The best responses integrated context with detailed knowledge of the text and were fully aware of Dickens’ construction of the characters and events to reflect his views on social reform.
c720u20-nov20-22-q:
In a unique series, given the exceptional context of 2020, the vast majority of candidates studied A Christmas Carol. A small minority studied The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

The Paper

The questions worked across all texts for all abilities. At the lower end, there was a tendency towards unfocused narrative but most attempted to deal with the characters or themes reflected in the questions set. A majority of candidates produced well-supported, well thought out essays. There was clear engagement with the texts and sustained focus on the questions. As with Section A, the source-based response (or “exploding extract”) continues to be successful in offering apt support for a closed book, untiered exam.

As intended, the extracts provided a starting point for candidates and were, quite rightly, used in different ways. Some candidates included the extract at the start of their response; many used the extract as part of a chronological approach; and a small minority used it throughout their response, cross referenced with the wider text. All approaches were valid, and all were able to work satisfactorily for the individual candidates concerned. Very few did not use the extract at all, though some treated it with a light touch, preferring to focus on the wider text. This too was acceptable, although potentially a wasted opportunity. Relatively few candidates made no reference at all to the wider text.

There continue to be numerous film references, particularly in A Christmas Carol. Although common to this paper, this was perhaps to be expected even more this year, when teaching time may have been reduced.

Discussion of context (assessed as AO3 in Section B) was also varied, with a general feeling that while many candidates had knowledge of a text’s contextual issues, they were often less secure in how to integrate this knowledge into their responses. Again, this could be a consequence of less preparation time and a lack of practise and feedback that would have allowed them to refine skills before the exam took place.

Comments on individual questions

c720u20-nov20-26-q:
The question focused on the conflict between Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde and the way it is presented in the novel. The question called on candidates to select key events to demonstrate understanding of the conflict between the two characters and comment on how Stevenson presented this in the story.

The extract was commonly used as a starting point to candidates’ essays, as it deals directly with the conflict caused by Dr Jekyll’s dilemma in choosing between his two “natures”. There was plenty of detail in the extract which reflected the conflict between the two characters, including discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of both natures. Most candidates were able to comment on Dr Jekyll’s dilemma and the temptation of becoming Mr Hyde. Nearly all were able to comment on the range of emotion Dr Jekyll demonstrated in response to some of Mr Hyde’s actions. A discriminator tended to be whether candidates were also able to explore ideas of conflict linked to moral weakness, sin and temptation as referenced towards the end of the extract.

The open nature of the question gave candidates of all abilities something to discuss and allowed candidates free reign to select the events they considered important in showing this conflict between the characters. Invariably, some weaker candidates responded narratively and simply retold the story, though most had some focus on the question. Other candidates tracked confidently through the novel, selecting key events such as the violent acts committed by Mr Hyde, the involuntary transformation between “natures” and the struggle between good and evil.

Some candidates discussed with engagement and evaluation the ways in which some of the views expressed were typical of those in Victorian society. There was less reference to context in a “bolted on” sense and it was pleasing to see at the top, engaging discussion of the symbolism of the conflict between the two characters. Discussion such as this allowed many candidates to discuss AO3 purposely and explore the struggle between good and evil and the morality of Victorian Britain.

The best responses integrated context with detailed knowledge of the text and were fully aware of different accounts and perspectives within the novel. At the highest level, responses discussed the construction of the characters and events and the way the text reflects views on the role of science and drugs in Victorian society.

Summary of Key Points

Points to remember:

• The first key question for the examiner is: ‘Does the candidate know the text well?’ • The second key question for the examiner is: ‘Has the candidate answered the question in a focused and sustained way?’ • AO2 and AO3 are worth a third of the marks but are not expected to take up a third of the essay

Characteristics of good Section B essay responses:

• Clear and sustained focus on the question asked • Use of the extract at a relevant point of the essay • Selection of short references to support points made • Coverage and reference to a range of relevant points across the wider text • Critical probing of inferences, implicit meanings and subtext as well as more surface ideas • Close analysis of how the language, writer’s techniques in the extract and wider text help to present the focus of the question • Clear appreciation of how contextual factors influence characters and themes • Suitable analytical style of writing

Ways in which performance could be improved:

• Plan where coverage of the extract will be best placed in the essay • More detailed coverage of the extract and wider text, particularly including details from the end of the text • More selection of detailed supporting references rather than general impressions • Avoid unfocused narrative and retelling of the story by selecting key events and characters • Keep sustained focus on the question • More focused and integrated discussion of how contextual factors influence writers’ characters, themes and ideas. Avoid contextual ‘bolt-ons’ • Avoid reference to plays and films when discussing prose texts • Practise and develop an analytical style of essay writing
c720u20-nov20-31-q:
Watching a Dancer, by James Berry, elicited a wide variety of responses. There was widespread understanding of the key ideas and this led to engagement with the very familiar subject matter of performance.

Only a minority of candidates linked the poem to their own experiences, though some made a link to performing in their own lives or watching others on stage. Some also discussed the importance of music in their own lives as a way to escape and relax.

Candidates clearly enjoyed the poem and nearly all saw the poem as a positive portrayal of the dancer, from the point of view of both the performer and the audience. Often, the dance was seen as a balletic performance and there was a keen sense of the athleticism of the performer through selection of “shapely and strong”. There was often productive and valid discussion by candidates of the possible symbolism of the “red costume”.

The best candidates commented on the structure of the poem in terms of the anticipation and progression of the dance, with particular attention paid to the stillness in the second stanza and the possible nerves and excitement evoked by Berry in this section. Many discussed the repeated use of the pronoun “she”, often linking this with a sense of self, or extreme scrutiny from the viewpoint of the audience. The majority of the candidates showed an appreciation of the skill of the dancer in performing and the imagery of her swimming and flying. Many explored the effect of the music on her body, with some thoughtful discussion of “pulses” evoking heartbeat and blood pumping and “haunts” linking to ideas of fear and possession.

Overall, Watching a Dancer worked very well, with candidates finding the poem accessible and giving them opportunities to show thoughtful insight and sensitivity.
c720u20-nov20-32-q:
The pairing of Watching a Dancer and The Busker gave the candidates plenty to discuss in terms of comparison and worked well across the entire ability range. The Busker was well understood, with many candidates recognising the central idea of the violinist playing on the street for money, with mixed success. However, the poem also raised some misreadings, such as the man being a dancer or a puppeteer (due to the “dancing spider”). There was also confusion over whether the musician was extremely skilled or very poor. Both interpretations were rewarded, depending on the level of engagement and support provided. Candidates who had a clear understanding of the central idea in both poems were able to present sensible, justifiable interpretations and readings of both poems.

Better responses were those who explored the metaphor of “old, mechanical toy” and probed the imagery of this in terms of the busker’s appearance and movements. The sounds of the violin were referenced through “scratches” and “grating”, with these usually explored sensibly as having negative effects on the listener. The skill of the violinist was often discussed, with his two hands working in isolation. Better answers explored the images of a “dancing spider” on its web and the delicate implications of “a lady taking tea”. At the very top, there was discussion of the violence of the movements, through appreciation of onomatopoeic language as well as phrases such as “dangerous little stabs” and “point blank”. There was some apt discussion on the success of the busker in terms of the word sparingly”, as well as his main audience being the pigeons who largely ignore him. However, the end of the poem was generally not well discussed and often ignored.

Most candidates made thoughtful links and contrasts between the poems. This often centred around the environment of the performance and the skill of the performers. Many contrasted the fluidity of the first performer with the more jerky, staccato feel of the second. Many commented on the poems’ apparent messages of various levels of appreciation for performers.

Overall, candidates dealt well with the poems and levels of engagement were high.

Summary of Key Points

Characteristics of good poetry responses:

• A thorough examination of the first poem in 3.1 • A thorough examination of the second poem in 3.2, either as a discrete element or as part of the comparison • Clear comparison of ideas, mood and some reference to how the poets use language • Detailed selection and coverage from each poem • Comments exploring the meaning of these selections • Spending about an hour on the poetry questions

Ways in which performance can be improved: • Ensure that the first poem is adequately analysed in 3.1 • Ensure that the second poem is adequately analysed in depth in 3.2 • Practise commenting on a range of poems and poetic techniques, including imagery and figurative language • Avoid spotting and labelling techniques and patterns with no reference to meaning • Develop the use of supporting references to support understanding of subtext • Avoid ‘over reading’ of hidden meanings in the poems • Experience in reading poems where similar topics are handled differently by poets • Rehearse timings across the exam to ensure sufficient time is given to the poetry

Most candidates answered the question with comments on both Romeo and Benvolio, but were able to do equally well if they focused on Romeo. Those that correctly placed the extract could usually comment effectively on the difference between Romeo and his feelings for Rosaline here and later in the play, when his feelings towards Juliet are arguably more genuine and certainly more requited. However, a significant minority of candidates incorrectly assumed that that “her favour” was a reference to Juliet rather than Rosaline. The majority of candidates wrote successfully on Benvolio, regarding him as a kindly, supportive confidante to his friend, although surprisingly few commented on his ulterior motive in finding out information about Romeo’s sadness for the benefit of Lord and Lady Montague.

The extract provided ample opportunity for language analysis. Less able candidates were able to pick out features such as Romeo’s torrent of oxymorons, the repetition of ‘O’ and use of the third person “This is not Romeo” to suggest his emotional confusion. The short lines and rapid interchange of comments at the opening of the extract gave candidates the opportunity to comment on structure, as did the rhyming couplets towards the end. Some confusion was caused by lines such as “love, whose view is muffled still, / Should without eyes see pathways to his will”, and there was a divergence in opinion regarding the sincerity of Benvolio’s “No, coz, I rather weep”. Many misinterpreted Benvolio’s cry of “Soft!” as an insult, adding to a view of Romeo’s effeminacy which seemed to feed into rather sweeping and mostly unproductive discussion of Elizabethan gender roles.

More successful responses showed some appreciation of the fact that this is an audience’s first sight of Romeo, and were able to discuss potentially differing views: that some might respond sympathetically to this sensitive, wounded romantic dealing with rejection, while others might feel less positively towards his self-obsession and propensity for melodrama. They tended to go beyond the spotting of oxymorons and unpick the language of phrases such as “feather of lead,”, “heavy lightness” and “bright smoke”. Some found success in exploring the links between the recent “fray” and link to “Loving hate”. Weaker responses tended to be less secure regarding the identity of Romeo’s love and struggled to go beyond identifying some obvious language techniques such as the oxymorons. Some neglected the latter part of the extract, or struggled to select and comment on individual words and phrases and their effects, despite the rich array of images to choose from here.

This was an extremely accessible question which offered candidates a wide range of material to work with, and examiners felt that most responded with enthusiasm. A wide range of approaches were taken: some tracked conflict throughout the play in chronological order, mostly relying on the physical acts of conflict, while others identified different types of conflict presented in the play, including inner conflict and conflict within the family. As a result, examiners felt that responses were generally effective in tackling the question. Popular scenes included the opening brawl, with its involvement of the feuding families at all levels, from servants to patriarchs and the introduction of Tybalt and Benvolio, and Act 3 Scene 1, including the violent deaths of Mercutio and Tybalt. Lord Capulet’s row with Tybalt in Act 1 Scene 5 was also fertile ground for discussion, as was his conflict with Juliet in Act 3 Scene 5, with better responses here taking in Juliet’s inner conflict as an obviously religious and until now obedient daughter potentially being forced to commit bigamy. Other moments of internal conflict were Juliet’s reaction to Romeo killing Tybalt, her soliloquy in Act 4 Scene 3 prior to taking the potion and the lovers’ suicides in Act 5 Scene 3. It was good to see how many candidates discussed the death of Paris earlier in that scene, given its omission from the most popular film version of the play. Overall, examiners were impressed with the sheer range of valid examples of conflict from across the text.

Candidates were usually able to quote effectively from the play, with well-used quotations including “ancient grudge”, “Peace? I hate the word…”, “a plague a’both your houses”, “fire- eyed fury” and “My fingers itch”. Stronger responses were able to utilise such references for analysis, thus ensuring coverage of AO2 with word and sentence level comments added to the identification of turning points and comments on how conflict drives the narrative of the play. Better responses also often featured consideration of the ending and the resolution of the conflict, with its heavy cost. Higher ability candidates were also able to explore how family honour and toxic masculinity feed into the play’s conflicts. Weaker responses tended to concentrate on only one or two scenes, or attempted to utilise the extract to write about Romeo’s inner conflict relating to Rosaline without offering much more. Overwhelmingly, though, it was a narrative approach without attention to AO2 that was the mark of weaker answers to the question, and this remains the main area for development in essay responses on the play.

Candidates were clearly very familiar with this extract and found it accessible. Examiners were impressed by the levels of engagement and enthusiasm shown in many responses. As a relatively brief extract, it seemed to help candidates achieve decent coverage in the time given, and Lady Macbeth’s dominance in terms of the proportion of her lines in the conversation encouraged exploration of the dynamic of their relationship at this early point in the play. Many noted the strength of the relationship between the Macbeths, with “my dearest love” frequently cited, with better answers exploring Lady Macbeth’s praise “Great Glamis, worthy Cawdor, / Greater than both...” and seeing the emerging ambition and manipulation behind these epithets. Tracking of Lady Macbeth’s manipulation of her husband often took in her envisioning the “future in the instant” and her use of imperatives. Inevitably, the key image “Look like the innocent flower / But be the serpent under’t” was utilised by most candidates, who looked at its implications and connotations to varying degrees. However, some went into excessive contextual detail about the Gunpowder Plot, which merely served as a distraction. The line, “We shall speak further” caused some healthy debate, with some seeing it as evidence of Macbeth’s desire to make further plans and others interpreting it as evidence of Macbeth’s hesitancy and desire to put off Lady Macbeth's plan to kill Duncan.

Many candidates discussed the presentation of the non-typical gender roles displayed in the extract and the potential reaction from a Shakespearean audience, which is absolutely valid. However, there was a tendency for these comments to be sweeping and lacking subtlety. A number of candidates insisted on seeing this first interaction between the protagonists on stage entirely through the lens of Jacobean gender roles, which proved a rather reductive approach and, ultimately, self-limiting.

Stronger responses tracked the extract closely and noted how Lady Macbeth was able to use a range of tactics to drive her plan forward, convincing and manipulating Macbeth along the way. Some candidates recognised the echoes of the witches in Lady Macbeth’s greeting and linked this effectively to her presentation here. Some noticed the increased assertiveness of Lady Macbeth once Duncan’s plans were established, and traced the means of her manipulation closely, along with thoughtful discussion of Macbeth’s ambiguous final line.

Weaker responses tended to deal only with surface meaning or only selected a small number of references to discuss. Some candidates mis-placed the extract as occurring before the murder of Banquo, while others seemed to think that the plan to murder Duncan had already been established before this point. There was a tendency for some weaker responses to move outside the extract, either to reference Lady Macbeth’s soliloquy earlier in the scene or to discuss her emasculation of Macbeth in Act 1 Scene 7.

This question allowed candidates of all abilities to respond, with examiners commenting on the high level of engagement with the theme of guilt in the play. Key areas explored by candidates included Macbeth’s immediate response to Duncan’s murder and his inability to wash his hands; “sleep no more” and “amen” as further indicators of remorse; Banquo’s ghost; Lady Macbeth’s sleepwalking scene and Macbeth’s initial refusal to fight Macduff at the close of the play. Many candidates, quite reasonably, considered situations showing a lack of guilt, for example Lady Macbeth’s initial ease after Duncan’s murder.

A variety of approaches proved successful, with some focusing only on Macbeth and Lady Macbeth, whilst others included other relevant characters such as Macduff and Banquo. Candidates were, for the most part, confident in discussing the development of the theme across the whole play and were able to support their points with valid textual references. Popular quotations for discussion included “Neptune’s ocean” contrasted with “a little water” in the aftermath of Duncan’s murder, “never shake thy gory locks at me” in the banquet scene and “all the perfumes of Arabia” and “Out damned spot!” from Act 5 Scene 1. The inclusion of a contemporary view of regicide in many responses showed that context, although not required here, can be used to illuminate discussion without diluting focus. Overall, examiners were impressed by candidates’ thorough knowledge of the play and the amount of thought that had gone into many responses.

8 More successful responses had good coverage of the play, were focused on the theme throughout and selected relevant supporting scenes or quotations to highlight their ideas. Often, they were able to see signs that Macbeth feels guilt before the murder of Duncan and explore the linguistic clues that led them to this view. Many showed an overview by comparing the guilt shown by Lady Macbeth to that of Macbeth across the text. Those that considered motifs such as sleep and blood to be symbols of guilt, and explored how they were used throughout the play, did well. Some sensitive candidates were able to see Macbeth’s journey from guilt to nihilism in the latter stages, while others showed their perceptive understanding by exploring Macduff’s sense of guilt in contrast with Macbeth’s. Typically, higher level answers were those that were able to incorporate word and sentence level analysis of language and structure into sustained, secure discussion.

Weaker responses tended to either only manage partial coverage of the play or struggled to offer specific moments in support of generalised discussion. Some became unnecessarily embroiled in historical context, particularly concerning the Gunpowder Plot. There were issues with recognising the order of events (the “dagger” speech frequently occurring after Duncan’s murder) and correctly attributing key lines, with “Neptune’s ocean” frequently getting mixed up with “all the perfumes of Arabia”. …

Examiners saw a wider a range in quality for this question than at any point since 2017. Candidates tended to respond with enthusiasm to an extract featuring the arch-manipulator Iago and there was a strong sense of recognition of the character and his traits here, although some struggled to track his thoughts through the soliloquy. Quite a few responses incorrectly placed the extract as Iago’s first soliloquy at the end of in Act 1, and therefore started off on the wrong foot. However, there were also sensitive responses that showed perceptive understanding of Iago’s intentions and were able to make evaluative comments on the motives he offers to the audience. Key phrases for analysis included the apparently contradictory phrases “The Moor… / Is of a constant, loving, noble nature”, and “The lusty Moor / Hath leaped into my seat”, along with “like a poisonous mineral, gnaw my inwards” and “wife for wife”. Much was made of Iago’s jealousy and misogyny in this speech.

4 Stronger responses were able to make points about Iago’s manipulation of Roderigo before the start of the soliloquy by commenting on his use of imperatives and prose; they then tended to track Iago’s thoughts concerning the three characters to be enmeshed in his plot, along with the possible motives he gives us. They made a range of well-chosen selections for analysis, wisely avoiding taking much of what Iago says at face value. The use of the rhyming couplet and stage direction at the end were apt references to end with.

Weaker responses were generally able to pick up on Iago’s jealousy and desire for revenge and could show an awareness of how he plans to manipulate Cassio, Desdemona and Othello. However, for some there was confusion at times, particularly over whom he calls “this poor trash of Venice”. Some understood the idea of a soliloquy but were unable to link this with Iago’s character and purpose. Most were at least able to see the racist language and stereotyping in phrases such as “the lusty Moor” and comment on the extreme language used to foreshadow Othello’s fall, such as “a jealousy so strong / That judgement cannot cure” and “even to madness”.

This was an open-ended question, giving candidates a free choice. As a result, a wide range of approaches was taken, with some discussing one character only, whilst others looked at several and (usually) decided who they felt deserved the most sympathy. Desdemona elicited the most sympathy from candidates, with many detailed and perceptive essays focused entirely on her. Emilia was proposed by some, and there were some excellent essays arguing her case. Many candidates drew on discussions around feminism, misogyny and male violence against women, showing the play has a clear current relevance to students. Emilia was proposed as a feminist character who gives Desdemona a voice when she can no longer defend herself, with Act 3 Scene 4 and Act 4 Scene 3 featuring in support. Othello was also a popular choice, although elsewhere candidates argued he deserved little sympathy. Those candidates who were sympathetic towards Othello discussed racist slurs and his mistreatment by other male characters, again highlighting the current relevance of the play. Cassio and, perhaps worryingly, Iago were also nominated for sympathy, although here candidates tended to struggle to offer the level of support necessary for a satisfying response.

Popular moments and quotations included “green eyed monster”, Othello striking Desdemona, the characters’ deaths, the willow song, “ocular proof” and the handkerchief. Iago featured almost universally, as it is difficult to write about sympathy in the play without drawing on the villain. Dramatic irony was covered by many candidates in reference to various parts of the play.

Better responses tended to track the chosen character(s) across the whole play, regularly selecting textual references for analysis and identifying key moments that create sympathy. As in previous years, there were plenty of Band 4 and 5 responses that were confidently constructed and written, and many candidates were able to make well-supported evaluative comments to support their viewpoint. Weaker responses tended to be limited in the selection of scenes and relatively brief. Some otherwise sound discussions were held back somewhat by a limited range of quotations, while others selected a wide range of characters to discuss but, as a result, diluted the focus and reduced the opportunities for showing deeper levels of understanding and AO2 analysis.
c722u10a-jun22-41-q:
This question offered candidates one of the most comic moments from the play to write about and most candidates engaged fully with its events and subtext. Most were able to place the extract correctly, although a small minority thought that Beatrice had already been tricked by this point. Benedick’s damascene moment begins with dramatic irony (“This can be no trick”) that many picked up on, and the soliloquy offered a series of rhetorical questions and striking phrases to analyse for AO2 such as “I will be horribly in love with her” and “the world must be peopled”. The entrance of Beatrice provided candidates with fresh dramatic irony and humour and examiners were impressed with effective discussion from some candidates that contrasted the characters’ attitudes towards each other.

More successful responses made use of the stage direction at the start, which helped place the extract and show understanding of the events that lead up to this moment. Humour is never easy to analyse, but many candidates clearly understood how the scene works and selected some apt reference for analysis. A number of strong responses correctly identified that Benedick is mirroring his earlier speech when he labels Beatrice “fair… virtuous… wise” here, providing plausible evidence that he has loved her all along. Another feature of better responses was a good balance between comment on the soliloquy and the dialogue, seeing the effect this shift might have on an audience.

Less successful responses seem to ignore Benedick’s soliloquy and instead concentrated on the exchange with Beatrice, which limited the opportunities to show understanding and analyse textual detail. A few thought that Benedick was speaking in verse, while a significant minority wanted to move outside the extract to discuss Beatrice and Benedick’s behaviour elsewhere in the play. A small number of responses could grasp the situation, but passed up the opportunity to analyse language choice, thus missing out on AO2 marks.

This was an accessible question which elicited a wide range of responses. The numerous references to friendship and relevant events in the play enabled candidates at all levels to find something to write about. Some candidates took “friendship” to mean “relationship”, and so some discussion was perhaps tenuous, particularly when discussing Claudio and Hero or Hero and Leonato. Some discussions of Beatrice and Benedick worked well though, with candidates seeing an unconventional friendship that turns into love. Better selections included Claudio and Don Pedro, Claudio and Benedick and Beatrice and Hero. Don John, Borachio and Conrade made quite a few appearances, sometimes contrasted with the more genuine friendships in the play. Male friendships were discussed in relation to the male code of honour and the ways in which loyalty drives the plot (Claudio and Don Pedro) or love overcomes loyalty (Benedick). “Kill Claudio” was a key quotation utilised to discuss more than one friendship in the play.

Stronger responses tended to focus closely on “friendship” rather than romantic or familial relationships. There were some well-constructed discussions of the friendships between the women in the play and the ways in which they protect and trust each other, particularly in the face of misogyny, toxic masculinity, and women’s lack of agency within patriarchal Messina. Although there are no explicit marks for context, the reference to these issues often strengthened the response. Some responses contrasted female friendships with male relationships which appear to be hollower and more superficial. Weaker responses tended to not focus clearly on “friendship”, preferring to discuss romantic relationships, or struggled to select a range of relevant events and quotations. Some candidates showed understanding, but neglected AO2, therefore limiting their overall mark.
c722u10a-jun22-51-q:
This extract from the siege of Harfleur gave candidates an opportunity to engage with one of the most famous speeches in the play, and the vast majority of candidates were clearly familiar with it. Henry’s rallying speech provided a range of images and devices for them to get to grips with, and most understood the tone and purpose. The use of repetition (“Once more”, “On, on”, “English”, “England”), imperative verbs and personal pronouns offered plenty of potential for accessible analysis, as did the zoomorphic images to suggest fierceness and hunting prowess.

5 Stronger responses fully appreciated the significance of the speech, his first inspirational address to his army in the play, and its rhetorical power. They were able to track methodically through the extract, making thoughtful comments and analysing linguistic choices and structural devices as they went. They tended to make the most of the climactic ending to the speech, highlighting Henry’s motivational skill. Weaker responses tended to include some misunderstanding, confusing this with the speech before Agincourt or struggling to interpret lines such as “And sheathed their swords for lack of argument”. They also tended to work through the speech, offering a “translation” of some key lines but without commenting on the language choices and their effects. In a few cases there seemed to be some confusion between the words “patriarchal” and “patriotic”, although the nature of the speech meant that examiners generally understood which they meant.

This question offered candidates the opportunity to write about a range of characters in a play dominated by one man – even if, as ever, it was impossible for them not to write about Henry while doing so. They responded with some enthusiasm, with Canterbury and Ely’s mostly successful attempts at influencing Henry at the start of the play a popular starting point. The Dauphin’s provocation of Henry with the tennis balls was seen as a key influence, with candidates contrasting the two characters effectively. The Eastcheap characters featured in many responses, as did the treacherous lords, Bates and Williams and Katherine. Several candidates argued that Henry’s army were a key influence. Two unexpected individuals – though not “characters” – were also discussed as having affected and influenced Henry: his father and God.

Better responses were able to select key characters from different points across the text and argue why they had influenced or affected Henry, supported with well-chosen quotations. They tended to identify key moments of influence as turning points in the play as well as select key images and phrases to analyse to address AO2. Less successful responses tended to be brief or not select more than a couple of characters (or groups of characters) to discuss. Some approached the question through narrative which highlighted some influences on Henry along the way but struggled to discuss key moments in detail or select quotations for specific comment.
c722u10a-jun22-61-q:
This extract was from a key area of the text and seemed to be almost universally recognised, although the quality of responses varied quite widely, with some tracking the narrative on a fairly basic level, while others explored the dynamic between the new couple and probed the levels of meaning and motives on display. There was plenty of discussion of the position of women in this society and the submissive role that Portia was expected to play here, with some candidates making the point that Portia dominates the exchange to a surprising degree given her claim to be an “unlessoned… unschooled, unpractised” girl! Higher achieving responses were able to cover both speeches in the extract, evaluating the sincerity or otherwise of each character’s pronouncements. Most of these could see what the hyperbole of this set piece is masking and understood the significance of Portia’s “gift” of the ring. Weaker responses tended to track the speeches on a surface level, identifying techniques such as tricolon or hyperbole but without really making inferences, thus presenting the view that Portia is genuinely deeply in love with Bassanio, who would willingly die for her – despite evidence of Portia’s duplicity and Bassanio’s untrustworthiness elsewhere in the play.

Summary of key points

Characteristics of good extract responses: • clear and sustained focus on the question asked and on the details in the extract • selection of short, apt references to support points made • critical probing of inferences, implicit meanings and subtext as well as more surface ideas • wide-ranging coverage of the extract • close examination of how the language/imagery used helps to convey meaning.

Ways in which performance could be improved: • more detailed coverage of the extract, managing comment on the beginning, middle and end, not straying beyond it • more selection of supporting references rather than general impressions • more practice on probing subtext and interpreting what is really going on in the extract • less reference to contextual factors when AO3 is not addressed in this question • practice in responding to both soliloquies and extracts with characters interacting and responding to each other

6 Comments on individual questions – Essay Questions

As usual, essay questions focused on key themes and characters in the plays, and each one enabled students of all abilities to demonstrate their knowledge. Weaker candidates tended to track the narrative and find some points of focus, and it was encouraging that most were also able to offer some relevant, direct references from important moments in the play they had studied. For a closed-book exam, this was impressive, and highlights how most candidates were well-prepared. For some, though, the process of selecting some key words from these references for comment on their connotations and effects would have significantly increased their marks for AO2.

The challenge for higher ability students was to plan and execute a focused, analytical response, selecting the most pertinent references in support. Examiners saw a wide variety of successful approaches, and this year many noted an increase in evidence of planning, which is to be encouraged. Over the forty minutes recommended for the essay question, a five-minute plan can prove to be a time saver and it certainly enables candidates to maintain a clear focus and respond to the question in a logical, coherent manner. Better responses were characterised by tracking across the whole text chronologically and the ability to select and comment on key moments and quotations from relevant scenes. Weaker responses tended to be brief or often did not cover the whole play. Other less successful answers did not manage to incorporate AO2 elements into discussion. Probing effects of language choice and use of imagery were extremely productive sources of AO2 reward; another was the highlighting of turning points or key moments in the development of a character or theme.

Contextual discussion in the Shakespeare essay was often extremely relevant, for example how ideas of honour and contemporary gender roles contribute to conflict in Romeo and Juliet. However, some candidates allowed contextual explanation to dominate their responses. It is worth reinforcing the message to candidates that AO3 is not explicitly rewarded in this question, although it can add to credit for AO1 when it is focused and proportionate. In many cases, however, more attention to AO2 would enable better marks, and this, overall, needs to be a higher priority when teaching students how to respond to essay questions.

For AO4, examiners saw the whole range of performance. The five marks available for this in the essay question make up a significant proportion of the total. Encouragingly, there was clear evidence of proof-reading and correction in some scripts. As in previous years, a lack of capital letters for names lost marks, as did the absence of punctuation and the misspelling of character names. This year, examiners cited over-long sentences and a tendency for candidates to use an informal register to be factors too – perhaps consequences of a relative lack of exam practice when compared to previous summer series. An increasing tendency to abbreviate character names to initials, presumably to save time, is an unwelcome development that reduces formality and risks losing marks.

Responses to this question showed engagement from across the ability range, and examiners felt that candidates offered focused discussion of a range of characters in their responses, suggesting perhaps that most of the characters were seeking revenge in some way or other. …

The question about violent events allowed students of all abilities to access the paper.

The extract was a powerful one and engaged candidates: most explored the symbolism of the breaking of the conch and Piggy’s death as presented in the extract. This provided many opportunities for AO2 exploration and many candidates focused on the violent language and the description of Piggy’s death.

13 Outside the extract, most candidates wisely chose to focus on the key events demonstrating violence: the first pig killing, Simon’s death and the raid to snatch Piggy’s glasses were popular areas for discussion. Others tended to explore the theme through key characters (Ralph, Jack, Roger, Simon and Piggy) or through the changing relationship between Ralph and Jack. Jack was a popular topic of discussion, with candidates examining his personality and how it changes, and how he acts as a catalyst for violence in the others.

Wider areas for discussion often included the significance of the fire; the idea that the beast is actually inside the children; animal imagery; and how the violent events mark the descent into savagery. More able candidates considered the theme of good versus evil; the setting and the damage done to the island by the plane crash; and the spectre of war taking place in the world beyond the island. As always, those who selected from across the novel fared the best.

Sometimes, contextual details were included. While these were not explicitly assessed in this question, they were often used meaningfully to discuss the question. Occasionally, the context was bolted on and was included unnecessarily.

A very small minority of candidates studied this text. Most responses were tackled ‘unseen’, with very little knowledge or understanding of Syal’s presentation of Meena’s experiences of growing up in Tollington. Many confused Anita with Meena and obviously had very limited understanding of the question.

Those few candidates that did study this enjoyable text engaged well with its characters, events and themes. The best candidates selected well from the text to show and understanding of how Meena ‘grows up’ in the novel. The extract provided a good opportunity to contrast Meena’s relationship with papa compared to mama, and explore their views and contribution to her development. This was a sensible starting point for candidates to explore how Meena’s relationship with her parents changes as she grows up.

Other rich areas for discussion included Meena’s changing relationship with Anita; how Nanima’s arrival and subsequent stay changes Meena’s viewpoint; and her stay in hospital with Robert.
