A small minority of candidates studied this text. The question provided an ideal opportunity for candidates to demonstrate their knowledge of the events and characters of the novel. Responses offered a range of approaches and some very thoughtful and sensitive discussions on the theme of discovering truths.

The extract proved to be very accessible and a good opportunity to discuss the truth of the clones’ lives and the way this is gradually revealed in the extract and the rest of the novel. Many candidates sensibly dealt with it first and then used it as an opportunity to discuss the clones’ lives and purpose. Many candidates used the extract as a springboard into a discussion of the wider text and the discovery of Hailsham’s true purpose. Much was made of Miss Lucy’s revelation that “None of you will go to America … be film stars” and that the clones’ lives are “set out”. Additionally, there was often also interesting discussion of the way Ruth often obscures the discovery of truths and the way the discovery of truths affected the characters and their relationships.

14 Many candidates made clear links between the discovery of truths and the three stages of the novel. Some responses included sensitive handling of Part Three of the novel, as the characters discover the truth and reality of donating and becoming carers. There were also some effective links and evaluations made across the text including consideration of the tragic nature of the text.

Weaker responses tended to be heavily reliant on the extract with very little or no reference to the central theme and discovery about “cloning”. Weaker responses also tended to make sweeping statements and/or had little discussion about the wider text and/or latter stages of the novel. These responses tended to contain little commentary on events at the cottages or beyond this point.
c722u10b-jun22-04-q:
The question, on ghostly experiences in the novel, gave candidates a completely open opportunity to show off their knowledge of the events and characters of the novel.

There was a tendency to explore the extract first. This was perhaps sensible, as it provided a rich seam of exploration in terms of AO1 and AO2. The situation Arthur Kipps finds himself in; Hill’s use of Spider as a proxy for Kipps’ emotions; sound imagery; the feeling of the woman in black’s control, manipulation and temptation; the use of first person; and pathetic fallacy were all often explored well through a tracking and discussion of the extract. Occasionally, the extract was treated in an unseen way and, judging by the cautious references to “the narrator” and guesses about the identity of Spider, this was clearly the case in some instances. The powerful nature of Hill’s writing allowed the vast majority of the candidates to engage with the question, even those that did not address the whole novel.

In general, however, candidates seemed to have a really thorough knowledge of the text and were able to explore Kipps’ journey from London to Eel Marsh House and back again. Candidates wrote well about the early scenes at Mrs Drablow’s funeral, the pony and trap, and the woman in black’s appearance at the nursery window. A minority of candidates got to the very end of the book and these candidates also tended to reference the complex structure of the novel in terms of a ‘framed narrative’, impressively tying this in to the focus of the question.

Overall, it was very clear that those who wrote on this book really had enjoyed the experience of engaging with this genre. Inevitably, there were candidates who relied heavily on film adaptations of the novel and these were obvious because of discrepancies between the book and the film.

A final note in terms of SPaG (AO4): many candidates would benefit from learning the key words in the text. ‘Woman’, ‘Arthur’ and ‘Crythin Gifford’ were all frequently misspelled.
c722u10b-jun22-05-q:
Jeanette is central to the novel and the vast majority of candidates engaged well with the question identifying and discussing a wide range of valid “turning points” for the character.

Sensibly, many candidates used the question as an opportunity to discuss turning points framed by Jeanette’s relationship with her mother e.g., her initial adoption; being forced to attend school and her experiences there; her experiences of religion and church; the exploration of her sexuality and her relationships with women and her return home.

15 The extract was used to introduce Jeanette’s first meeting with Melanie and to then discuss their relationship at other points in the novel. Those that used the extract well noted the innocence of the girls at the start and what was to follow e.g., the fury of the pastor. Much was made of the reference to the shared experience of “no father” and the connection the girls felt as a result of this. Weaker candidates unhelpfully over-analysed the significance of “staring at the whelks”. The effect of the dialogue in the extract was often picked up as a device to reflect the nervous attraction / embarrassment of the girls.

Most candidates had a good sense of the key turning points which reflect Jeanette’s changing relationship with religion as she grows up, with the best candidates providing very detailed and nuanced examinations of events including the sermon on the nature of perfection and the pastor’s confrontation of Jeanette and Melanie’s relationship.

It was also pleasing to note the frequent references to the mythic elements of the novel, with these allegorical elements used to support the best responses.

Weaker candidates struggled to include a range of detail from across the whole text. Others spent much of their response focused on the relationship between Jeanette and Melanie, and whilst certainly relevant, these answers did not always remain clearly focused or provide sufficient discussion of turning points as an important theme in its own right.
c722u10b-jun22-06-q:
The question on conflict provided plentiful opportunities for candidates to discuss the theme. There were some very thoughtful discussions of the theme within the different relationships central to the text with the best reaching sensitive evaluation.

The extract proved helpful as it provided a springboard into some of the key points in the play, including Christopher’s difficult relationship with his father and his investigation into who killed Wellington.

Christopher’s reaction to his father’s touch was well discussed by candidates, who often went on to discuss his reactions to other similar events in the play. Most, sensibly, discussed Christopher’s reaction to finding the dog and his difficulty in coping when confronted by the policeman. Some candidates also included valid discussion of conflict resolution in the text such as the touching of fingers and thumbs in the extract. The best candidates also discussed the conflict that arises in Ed and Judy’s relationship in some detail and provided solid discussion of the conflict caused as a result of difficulties in raising and coping with Christopher. Many candidates at the top end also discussed the conflict that arises due to Christopher’s logic and interaction with other people in the play.

Many candidates addressed stylistic features, such as the breaking of the fourth wall, Christopher’s manner of speaking, and the use of stage directions. These all proved useful in gaining AO2 marks. Weaker candidates focused a little too simplistically on the physical fight between Christopher and Ed. Amongst weaker candidates there were many who made very few comments on the wider text, or briefly made reference to one or two other events in the play. Some candidates over relied on discussion of Christopher’s reaction to touch.
c722u10b-jun22-07-q:
Responses to this text were, on the whole, of a very high standard. The question provided plentiful challenge for candidates to discuss the character of Geof. The extract provided a good basis for some very confident and sensitive responses about Geof, many of which thoroughly explored the underlying tension between he and Helen.

There were some excellent sensitive and thoughtful discussions of the character which included the way Geof supports Jo at different points in the play. Candidates sensitively explored the breaking of gender stereotyping reflected in the extract and Geof’s plans to support Jo as her chosen birth partner.

Sensitive responses were able to extrapolate a discussion of the subtext of inverse sexism imbued in this section and other sections of the text. Some also commented on the way the extract exemplified Geof’s capitulation as a result of Helen’s manipulative nature throughout the play. Good responses commented on the end of the extract, also commenting on the way Geof (like other males) leaves Jo.

Outside the text, candidates often provided wider references to Geof’s relationship with Jo and how their relationship was mutually supportive. The best answers also linked the way Geof was treated by Jo as a cyclical result of her treatment by her own mother.

Weaker candidates lacked broader reference to the wider events in the play and stayed within the focus of the extract. Less successful answers misread the “frightening” presence of Geof and/or Helen without any of the context and nuance of Jo’s pregnancy. There were less instances of candidates referencing the 1961 film version rather than the original text, which cannot be valued as textual support by the examiner. Weaker responses also tend to focus on earlier events in greater detail and lose sight of the final scenes. There was also less reliance on context which has previously been problematic, such as the 1960’s setting and/or the characteristics of a kitchen sink drama.
c722u10b-jun22-08-q:
This was the most popular question on the paper in terms of candidate numbers. The question’s focus on the character of Eric Birling allowed the vast majority of students to readily engage with the extract and demonstrate secure knowledge of the text through detailed, focused and engaged responses. Even candidates at the lower end were able to achieve some success by engaging with the extract to support more basic ideas about Eric’s personality and interactions. Better candidates focused on the character at the beginning, end and various key points in between and explored his relationships with other characters. A minority of candidates muddled Eric with Gerald, sometimes attributing the actions of Gerald with that of Eric.

The character of Eric was often labelled as “alcoholic” and weaker candidates fixated on this aspect of Eric’s presentation, with sweeping, non-tentative statements about his perceived drinking problem. For some candidates, this took up a significant portion of their discussion of the character and became a little repetitive and undeveloped. Better candidates discussed his consumption of alcohol in a wider context, as a way of masking his guilt and difficult situation. They also acknowledged the role alcohol played in his treatment of Eva Smith.

17 Candidates often discussed what we learn of Eric from the play’s initial scene, including focused discussion of the stage direction, “half shy, half assertive” and how this might relate to his character’s development in the rest of the play. Many candidates were able to discuss Eric’s position in the Birling family: there was considerable exploration of Eric’s difficult relationship with Mr. Birling and, to a lesser degree, of his relationships with Sheila and Mrs. Birling.

Most candidates were aware that, at some point, Eric changes. Socialism and Priestley’s ‘message’ were discussed at some length, which was often tied to consideration of the differences between the two generations. At times, Priestley’s message became the main focus of candidates’ final sections, resulting in some lack of focus.

It is interesting to note how changes in society have led to a significant change in many candidates’ interpretation of the character. Eric no longer commands the near universal sympathy for his apparent remorse and change of heart at the end of the play. Instead, there was a much greater focus on his treatment of Eva Smith. Rape, toxic masculinity, gaslighting, dehumanisation and objectification were all discussed in great depth and to varying degrees of success by candidates. More able candidates discussed this in terms of how contemporary and modern audiences may have reacted to his words and actions.

Overall, this was a very successful question that elicited the full range of responses.
c722u10b-jun22-09-q:
Responses to this text were, on the whole, of a very high standard and it seems to be a text that is well chosen by centres who know their candidates’ ability to respond positively to its humour, themes and messages.

There was some excellent analysis of the extract which provided a useful way to discuss the character of Dakin. Candidates commented sensitively on the confident, flirtatious subtext of Dakin’s interactions with Irwin here. This often provided an excellent springboard into a wider discussion of Dakin’s witty, sexually charged language at different points in the play and the changing nature of Dakin’s loyalties to Irwin at the expense of Hector. The majority of responses combined this with a wide-ranging discussion of Dakin’s confidence, manipulation of others and his scornful response to Posner’s adoration.

Most responses moved beyond Dakin’s relationship with Irwin to evaluate his relationships with Hector and the other boys often in a detailed, mature and confident way. Most responses discussed Dakin’s views on the various teaching styles presented in the play; his role as the ‘leader’ of the boys and his views on women, including his use of warfare metaphor for his relationship with Fiona which was viewed by some in a modern context as a horrific objectification of women. Some responses commented on Dakin’s success in receiving an Oxford scholarship and his later career as a tax lawyer.

Weaker responses (and there were not that many) tended to over-simplify and be a little formulaic in their assessment, making assertions that Dakin is discussing history with Irwin; is a clown; is sexist. These responses tended to crowbar in discussion and quotes that they were determined to use (very often, these contained the swear words contained in the play).
c722u10b-jun22-10-q:
The question worked extremely well across the full range of abilities. The extract gave candidates a useful reminder of Mickey and Edward’s meeting aged ‘seven’. Weaker candidates used simple differences between the characters to support their responses. More able candidates were able to link ideas presented in the extract to the wider text and the way Edward and Mickey’s lives are different.

Most discussed the difference between the way Mickey and Edward speak. The best of these were able to focus on Edward’s confident, polite, educated and generous nature in contrast to Mickey’s boredom, petulance and suspicion. Weaker responses focused on Mickey’s swearing and Edward’s use of a dictionary.

Pleasingly, many candidates took a balanced, nuanced approach to the different lives of the twins. The majority had sympathy for Mickey, making references to the differences arising from the social class of the two characters. There was some discussion of how, despite their differences, Mickey and Edward are drawn together and share some similarities, e.g., the Blood Brothers pact and their relationship with Linda. Some responses included thoughtful discussion of the way the social differences between Mickey and Edward widen as they move into the later stages of their teenage years and into adulthood. There was some sensitive discussion of the breakdown in communication between Mickey and Edward in certain parts of the play as their lives diverge e.g., following Edward’s return from university; when Mickey goes to prison.

Blood Brothers seems to be a text that is particularly prone to some candidates taking a narrative approach, and these were self-penalising. Candidates should be given opportunities to take a more selective approach in order to avoid a simple, but often very long, retelling of the story.

Coverage of the text overall improved, however, full coverage was a slight issue this year. There were some improved references to songs such as ‘My Child’ and occasionally ‘That Guy’ but little else. Reference to the songs is an obvious way to access AO2 marks and they are an important aspect of the text. Many candidates did not comment on the ending in which Mickey bitterly and tragically recognises the difference between his life and Edward’s.

Context is not explicitly rewarded here but stronger candidates dealt with this efficiently, mentioning class, arguments about nature and nurture and poverty to support points they were making about the twins. Weaker candidates often wrote paragraphs about Liverpool’s perceived poverty or Margaret Thatcher’s policies. Very often, this contextual information was confused, with references that the play was “set in the time of the industrial revolution” and statements such as, “Poverty was quite popular in Liverpool in the 1980s” or, “Most of society was religious.” Sweeping generalisations and over simplified comments regarding rich and poor were also evident.

19 Summary of key points

Characteristics of a good response: • use the extract purposefully, highlighting key details that help focus on the question and provide useful AO2 comments • use the extract as a springboard into a wider discussion of the text • coverage will include discussion of events/key details at the end of the text • focus on well-chosen key events or scenes, significant characters/relationships to link to the question and wider themes • have a sustained focus and direct textual references with good coverage of the text (referencing events spanning the beginning, middle and ending of the story) • clear planning and progression of the response, with development of ideas and supporting references, rather than assertions and general impressions.

Ways in which performance can be improved: • candidates need to be clear whether the text studied is a play or novel and should discuss the text accordingly. • Remind candidates of the bullet points built into the start of every question and use them to shape responses. • Encourage candidates to be selective in their use of the extract to demonstrate their AO2 skills. There is no requirement on Component 2 to analyse the extract in detail. Instead, use the extract as a springboard for a wider discussion, with a few key words or images explored that can then be broadened to show knowledge and understanding of the whole text. • Avoid ‘over analysis’ of vocabulary. ‘Mrs Lyons says Edward was a ‘tiny baby’. The adjective ‘tiny’ suggests her problems and life with her husband were ‘tiny’. • Avoid repeatedly labelling or naming every word class. Be selective. Also, avoid forcing techniques and subject terminology into their responses to the extract – either incorrectly or very tenuously: ‘The use of a descending tricolon causes Ralph and Jack to seem much closer to each other’. Similarly, avoid focus on analysis of sentence length, punctuation features or more non- fiction rhetorical devices, which again, can be an unproductive use of the extract. It also would be better to avoid unnecessary terms such as semantic fields or lexical sets and replace them with simple reference to ‘words’ or ‘phrases’. • Contextual details should only really be included in Section A if relevant to the question and then still need to be closely tied to discussion of the characters, events and details. For example, Priestley’s intentions in writing An Inspector Calls were central to this year's task but still needed to be closely tied to discussion of the play. Too often, context is confused and very general (e.g., ‘During the 1960s, or the Industrial Revolution, women were seen as failures if they didn’t stay home and have babies’). These are not particularly helpful, relevant or accurate. • Encourage pupils to learn key spellings such as character names and authors, as well as key words associated with each text and so likely to be employed. …
c722u20a-jun22-71-q:
“Dulce et Decorum Est” seemed to be a popular choice with candidates, and examiners commented on the high levels of engagement and empathy the poem elicited in responses. There was plenty of material to work with to address all three assessment objectives, and the poem’s content was often explored in detail and with enthusiasm. Popular quotations for comment and analysis included the similes in the first stanza “like old beggars under sacks” and “coughing like hags”. From the second stanza “Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!” was well-used, and from the third much was made of “guttering, choking, drowning”, while the verb “flung” in the final stanza proved an effective selection. It was heartening to see a genuine enthusiasm for the poem and commitment to its message in many responses.

Examiners felt that there was less “technique-spotting” than in previous series, and it was good to see that most candidates could discuss the effects of language choices, although some noted that the tricolon or rule of three was often referenced without comment on its impact.

This is a poem that lends itself to understanding contexts, so, on the whole, candidates found they could address AO3 reasonably well. Nonetheless there was a minority of responses that offered little contextual information – even to the extent of not acknowledging that this is a poem about war, and some of those that did were not able to identify it correctly as World War One. However, most could, and many were able to reference Owen’s career as a serving officer, his experience of shell shock, his death close to the Armistice, the trenches, chemical warfare, his views on the tragedy of war and Jesse Pope. A few candidates referenced Craiglockhart and being influenced by Sassoon. Encouragingly, many were able to incorporate their discussion of context into their broader discussion of the poem.

Stronger responses tracked through the whole poem, managing coverage of elements of all four stanzas. They managed to integrate close analysis of key words, phrases and images into their discussion along with relevant contextual details. Weaker responses tended to be brief and were often confined to the first two stanzas, thus missing out on the opportunity to discuss the lasting effects of death on those left behind and Owen’s direct address towards those who perpetuated the “old Lie” through propaganda.
c722u20a-jun22-72-q:
The most popular selections for comparison were, understandably, poems about war, with “The Soldier”, “Mametz Wood”, “A Wife in London” and “The Manhunt” all frequent choices. “The Soldier” provided a useful counterpoint to the ideas in “Dulce”, as well as offering some contrasting biographical context on two writers who both ultimately lost their lives as a result of World War One. “Mametz Wood”, meanwhile, offered some obvious similarities, whilst also giving candidates the opportunity to explore the lasting effects of war, thereby creating a strong contrast with the more personal and immediate effects presented in “Dulce”. Examiners also saw effective comparisons with poems that feature “death” in differing, sometimes non-literal ways, such as “To Autumn”, “Hawk Roosting”, “Death of a Naturalist” and “Imperceptible as Grief”. The levels of success tended to vary with these poems, with direct textual support perhaps harder to produce, but examiners were pleased to encounter many thoughtful and individual responses.

As usual, stronger answers to 72 benefitted from candidates making appropriate choices for comparing the presentation of death, in particular where they knew their chosen poem well. This allowed them to develop their points with focus while incorporating close language analysis. The best answers sustained their focus on death in both poems and selected apt quotations to help them discuss meaning and language. At the top end of the mark scheme, some candidates explored ideas about death confidently and sensitively, with context interwoven into the comparison.

Weaker responses were often a result of an injudicious choice of the second poem, where comparison was forced or unfocused, or lacked the direct references required to construct a meaningful response. A number of otherwise decent responses were affected by not linking to context effectively in both poems being discussed. Sometimes when context was included it was via a bolted-on paragraph at the end of an answer, rather than being integrated and linked to the poems’ content.

Once again there was quite a lot of confusion between titles and contexts of war poems; it’s certainly worth revising the differences between these poems, as they cause both candidates and examiners problems when mixed up. Examiners also once again noted the fact that in 72 comments were often made on “Dulce” that had not been made in 71, with some candidates still seemingly reluctant to repeat themselves by including the same points on the first poem in both 71 and 72. It is again worth reminding students that they can score marks in both 71 and 72 for making the same supported point or piece of language analysis on the given poem.

Summary of key points

Characteristics of good poetry responses: • careful tracking of the poem set for 7.1, with detailed coverage of the whole poem • probing of subtext, tentative interpretation rooted in the poems • strong focus on imagery, language and the effects they create • interweaving of relevant contextual detail into discussion • sensible selection of poem to suit the theme for comparison in 7.2 • detailed, developed comparison of ideas, language and context in 7.2.

22 Ways in which performance can be improved: • more detailed coverage of the whole poem set in 7.1 • practice in supporting ideas with detailed reference to the poems • selection of an appropriate poem for comparison, with a strong focus on the theme of the question • effective revision of anthology poems to ensure the ability to recall and make good use of textual detail • practising a structured approach to comparison, ensuring effective coverage of both poems and detailed comparative comments in 7.2 iIncorporation of relevant contextual detail to support overall discussion in both 7.1 and 7.2.

The question focused on attitudes to poverty in the novel. This gave candidates of all abilities something to discuss and allowed even the weakest candidates to address contextual issues examined in AO3. There were relatively few that merely retold the story and most had some focus on the question. Lots of candidates tracked confidently through the extract, identifying the characters’ respective attitudes to Christmas as a starting point to their essay. Most candidates had an understanding of the role of the charity collectors and were able to contrast their attitudes and views with those of Scrooge. Better candidates were able to link the events of the extract with later events in the novella, such as Scrooge’s childhood and his attitudes to Tiny Tim. Weaker responses sometimes did not move much beyond the extract, though the vast majority made at least partial reference to wider characters and events.

The most successful candidates tracked Scrooge’s view of poverty through the novel, gave reasons for how and why it changed, and were able to accurately contrast his initial cold comments with the warmth and love he shows through his redemptive acts at the end, signalling his intention to eliminate the poverty he had caused. Although a minority of candidates only focused on the Cratchits and their Christmas dinner in terms of wider text, it was pleasing to see a significant number of references to Fred and his contrasting views of being poor at Christmas; the painful regret of Marley’s ghost; a real understanding of why Belle breaks off the engagement to Scrooge; and the purpose and significance of Ignorance and Want. Better candidates explored attitudes to poverty by the poor themselves: the Cratchits of course, but also how the actions of Mrs Dilber and the others at Old Joe’s shop are excused in their eyes by their circumstances.

Slightly weaker answers sometimes focused on the presentation of the poor in the novel rather than addressing the specific question of attitudes to them, but even this approach was not without some merit. Occasionally too, the answers drifted into attitudes to Christmas, and this was particularly true when bringing in Fezziwig and minor details such as the lighthouse keepers, the sailors and the miners and their attitudes to the season.

Contextual discussion was built into the question, meaning that very few candidates did not include some AO3 references. A majority selected the “surplus population”, “workhouses” and “prisons” in the extract to gain credit in this area. Many went on to link Scrooge’s views in the extract to Thomas Malthus, though spelling of his name and what he believed in varied greatly. Biographical information on Dickens was also well referenced, though inevitably the quality of this varied. Dickens’ own attitudes and view of poverty and the poor provided a rich seam of discussion for many candidates.
c722u20b-jun22-22-q:
Silas Marner works well for every level of ability, with its strong storyline, clearly delineated characters and accessible themes, as well as clear contextual features. The vast majority of responses were excellent. Most candidates were clearly well prepared and engaged with the relationship between Silas and Eppie in a highly evaluative way.

The extract was often well used as an exploration of Silas and Eppie’s early relationship, with candidates often using it as a starting point to discuss the closeness between the characters. There was much discussion of how the relationship reintroduced Silas to society and how he rediscovers his faith. Many candidates took the opportunity to explore AO2 points through the extract, with many picking up on phrases such as “convulsive joy” and “half sobbing”. It was particularly gratifying to see so many candidates picking up on the humour in the extract and exploring how this leads to a softening in Silas’s presentation.

25 Naturally, the imagery of Eppie’s first appearance to Silas and the symbolism of the timing, her golden hair, and placement on the hearth were all explored to great effect. Often, discussion of Silas and Eppie’s relationship led on to discussion of the important themes of parenting and responsibility. Most discussed Godfrey and Nancy’s inability to have children and thoughtfully explored his attempt to reclaim Eppie and the reasons of his failure to do so because of Eppie’s loyalty and love for Silas.

Most candidates used AO3 sensibly and at the top end this was perceptive and assured. Comments on biographical details about Mary Ann Evans and her own loss of faith, views on parenting and adoption were often integrated well into responses. Contemporary attitudes to adoption, gender roles and country and urban contrasts were also discussed in an illuminating manner.
c722u20b-jun22-23-q:
The question asked candidates to consider the presentation of the destruction and panic caused by the Martians in the novel. This gave candidates a completely open opportunity to show off their knowledge of the events and characters of the novel.

The extract focused on the Narrator’s observations of the mass migration triggered by the invasion and the destructive nature of the invading aliens. Whilst a minority of weaker candidates ignored or barely touched on the extract, most seized the rich opportunity to explore AO2. The best responses picked up on Wells’ contrast of the situation with historical events; the sheer scale of the exodus; use of alarming language such as “stampede”, “massacre of mankind” and “monstrous”; listing of affected areas of society; and the casual descriptions of death. The final paragraph provided candidates with a dense portrayal of panic and confusion and many candidates sensibly explored this in depth.

In terms of the wider text, the question allowed candidates the freedom to explore the ideas in any way they saw as appropriate. Many took the opportunity to discuss the panic as experienced by various characters, such as the curate, the artilleryman and the Narrator. Understandably, the incident of the curate’s breakdown was well explored by a number of candidates with great success. Other candidates took more of an event-based approach, focusing on the initial calmness and mild curiosity at the start of the novel and then tracking and contrasting the fear that followed. Lower band responses were inevitably quite generalised and commented on ways in which people panicked, but were not always linked to specific characters or incidents.

Discussion of the destruction and panic in the novel often also acted as a springboard for candidates to discuss a range of contextual details and explore AO3. There were some astute and valid references to war and the breakdown of society; survival of the fittest; Tasmania; the British Empire; and Imperialism which were often validly and skilfully used.
c722u20b-jun22-24-q:
Pride and Prejudice proved to be relatively popular once again, and was studied right across the ability range. There were some very able candidates studying this text and they responded well to the opportunities offered by the novel and the set question, which called on candidates to consider the presentation of the relationship between Elizabeth and Mr. Darcy in the novel.

26 Fewer candidates relied solely on the extract with only brief reference to the rest of the text. Responses were discursive although a minority of responses were without specific support from the text (either paraphrased reference to events or direct supporting reference). There was much discussion of the character’s “pride” and “prejudice”, often misplaced or bolted on, rather than the relationship between the characters. Some candidates were able to place the extract precisely, however this was rare as many candidates misread the extract as being taken from earlier in the novel rather than from the end.

The extract allowed many candidates to discuss both characters and their relationship. However, overall, there was limited exploration of AO2. Lower band responses did not comment on the extract other than to overly focus on Elizabeth’s “playfulness” and “liveliness of mind”. Many candidates took a “light touch” approach to the extract and/or discussed the relationship between Elizabeth and Mr. Darcy in a very superficial and general way. Many candidates successfully explored the relationship between the characters in contrast to the relationships between Mr. Collins and Charlotte Lucas; Jane and Bingley and Lydia and Wickham. More successful responses also explored Elizabeth and Mr. Darcy's relationship within a frame of expectations or prospects of marriage, rejection of marriage proposals or (in very few responses) their eventual marriage. Some candidates developed a discussion of Elizabeth by including reference to Darcy’s early opinions and prejudice towards Elizabeth and often tracked skillfully through the relevant events of the novel. The top band answers framed discussion of the characters’ relationship within an appreciation of Austen’s presentation of love, relationships and marriage.
c722u20b-jun22-25-q:
The question focused on marriage worked well for every level of ability and the majority of candidates were able to discuss the theme in a range of sustained, assured, confident and evaluative ways. The extract, and Jane’s reflection on her marriage, provided candidates with a springboard into the rest of their essay. Most, quite sensibly, dealt with it first, often then referring back to the beginning of the novel in order to track the development of Jane’s relationship with Rochester. AO2 was addressed with some success. Mid band responses commented on the happiness of Jane and Rochester’s marriage: their happiness; their being equals. Some responses focused on the religious tone of the extract and the “blest” nature of their marriage. There were a few responses which overly focused on Jane’s character rather than the theme of marriage.

Following discussion of the extract many candidates refocused on Jane’s earlier experiences and the build up to her marriage to Rochester. Many candidates somewhat unnecessarily discussed Jane’s childhood and the red room again using unhelpful symbolic interpretations (e.g., the room representing the ‘menstrual cycle’). Most candidates commented sensibly on Jane’s relationship with Rochester: as a governess and as a prospective wife, with higher band responses including marriage in light of not only Jane and Mr. Rochester but also St. John Rivers. Higher band responses often commented on other characters experience of marriage such as Blanche Ingram and Bertha Mason as examples of the way women were treated either in a standalone sense or in comparison to Jane. There were, however, a significant number of responses which did not feature any reference to Rochester’s marriage to Bertha Mason or potential marriage to Blanche Ingram which was a missed opportunity.

AO3 was mainly well integrated predominantly through comment on the extract. References to marriage, gender, religion, economic status, social class and sensitive parallels between Jane and the real-life situation of Charlotte Brontë were made. Indeed, Brontë’s views on women’s independence, and marriage for love and of equals often led to engaged discussion. Overall, this was a successful question for the candidates who studied the novel.
c722u20b-jun22-26-q:
The question focused on the presentation of shock and horror in the novel. This allowed candidates to respond in a variety of valid ways. Most candidates were aided by the extract which referred to Hyde’s violent actions, lack of remorse, effect on others and appearance: “It wasn’t like a man”. The extract provided a clear focus and springboard to discuss the shock and horror of Hyde’s character and actions and this proved useful to candidates. Film versions seemed to be much less prevalent this year, though they were still occasionally present.

Candidates engaged fully with the extract, discussion of which often led into the rest of the text. The majority of responses referenced key events e.g., the murder of Danvers Carew, Jekyll’s scientific experimentation and Dr Lanyon’s death. Hyde’s “black sneering coolness”, “dwarfish”, “troglodytic” appearance and violent actions: “trampling calmly” and his later “ape- like fury” were invariably cited and used to target AO2. Candidates often widened the scope of their discussions to include the reactions of others in order to discuss the shock and horror elicited by Hyde. The top band responses widened their scope to bring in features of Gothic horror which also contributed to the theme. Many candidates, surprisingly, did not mention the ending of the text and the shock and horror of Jekyll as a “self-destroyer” which was a missed opportunity.

On the whole, the use of context was secure, relevant and accurate and at its best, well developed and sensitively applied. Occasionally candidates used context to drive their essays, and whilst this can be a valid approach, it often limited reference to the whole text. There was less use of biographical information about Stevenson ‘bolted-on’. There was less reliance on discussions of Freud and the id and ego theories, however, there was an increased link between Jekyll and homosexuality which was sometimes limited unless framed within discussion of reputation and Victorian societal expectations. Better approaches tended to be discussion of the text linked to the ideas of Victorian respectability, desire, repression and hypocrisy; Darwin’s Theory of Evolution; the conflict between science and religion; the Victorian fascination with physiognomy; and links to contemporary literary trends all of which could be directly linked to, and exemplified by, textual details.

Summary of Key Points Points to remember: • the first key question for the examiner is: ‘Does the candidate know the text well?’ • the second key question for the examiner is: ‘Has the candidate answered the question in a focused and sustained way?’ • AO2 and AO3 are worth a third of the marks but are not expected to take up a third of the essay.

Characteristics of good Section B essay responses: • clear and sustained focus on the question asked • use of the extract at a relevant point of the essay • selection of short references to support points made • coverage and reference to a range of relevant points across the wider text • critical probing of inferences, implicit meanings and subtext as well as more surface ideas • close analysis of how the language, writer’s techniques in the extract and wider text help to present the focus of the question • clear appreciation of how contextual factors influence characters and themes • suitable analytical style of writing.

28 Ways in which performance could be improved: • plan where coverage of the extract will be best placed in the essay • more detailed coverage of the extract and wider text, including the beginning, middle and end • more selection of detailed supporting references rather than general impressions • avoid unfocused narrative and retelling of the story • more practice on subtext and interpretation • practise creating clear, cohesive arguments which address the question asked • more focused and integrated discussion of how contextual factors influence writers’ characters, themes and ideas. Avoid contextual ‘bolt-ons’ • careful adherence to the rubric requirements of the paper to ensure that candidates are only answering questions on the texts that they have studied • avoid reference to plays and films when discussing prose texts • practice and develop an analytical style of essay writing • handwriting must be legible.

c722u20c-jun22-31-q:
Home by Fran Landesman proved accessible to all candidates and there were a range of responses, right across the ability range. These included many original, thoughtful and personal responses to the poem. This was helped by the fact that the poem’s subject matter was highly relatable to candidates.

There were several different interpretations of the poem: all were valid readings and marked on their individual merits. Most candidates had the good sense to read and consider the poem before starting to write, but there were a number of responses that betrayed the fact that the candidate had not read, or had misread, the poem. These interpreted from the title and first line that the content would be wholly positive, then hastily realigned their answer once they worked out that the “Home” of the title was not the stereotypical haven of comfort and security they were led to expect. There were also many perceptive comments on the idea of Home meaning more than a physical building, and this set up a comparison to the second poem.

30 The majority of candidates selected and commented thoughtfully on a range of details in the poem. Many of Landesman’s phrases were explored: “hang your hat”, “can’t get a break”, “a test you always fail” and “where the heartache / Really started” were all often explored well. Many candidates identified with the criticism implied in ‘Too fat or too thin’ and the ‘endless argument[s]’. Indeed, the poem’s connections to contemporary issues, like body image, toxic relationships, and the lasting “triggering” effects of experiences made it a text with which they were able to understand and connect to, either on a highly personal level or as part of the current themes and concerns of society.

It was clear that many candidates had been well prepared for this task and there were forensic and sensitive discussions: for example, on the repetition of “but” and “always”, as well as explorations of the words “ought”, “endless” and “haunt”. Better candidates also noted the subversion of the cliched expressions in the poem and this proved to be a bit of a discriminator. These candidates often noted this as “sarcasm” or “mockery” and alluded to the bitterness in their use. The reference to “home sweet home” was another discriminator: many candidates struggled to understand this reference, though a number managed to discuss it by linking it to “No place like home” in The Wizard of Oz!

Unfortunately, a sizeable minority of responses demonstrated the “weighing and measuring” approach, by simply counting lines and syllables and spotting language features. These were rarely successful, but some did manage to relate these to the perceived message and mood of the poem.

Overall, there was an overwhelming sense that candidates had enjoyed writing about the poem and it was very successful in terms of determining ability across the ability range.

The pairing of Home and Coming Home gave the candidates plenty to discuss in terms of comparison and worked well across the entire ability range. Coming Home was well understood, with many candidates recognising the idea of returning home. However, the poem also raised some misreading, such as rekindling a previous relationship. Better responses were those who picked up on the subtext of the impact of absence on the home and the sense of bringing the house back to life and feeling “the house becoming home”. Many candidates commented on the presentation of the house as “drear” or “extinct”. Many candidates focused on the first half of Coming Home without venturing into the “garden” of the text presented in the latter parts of the poem. Top band responses engaged fully with the presentation of the garden in the poem, either through comment on the returnee as “rain-god” or the way the soil “hisses and yields”. The best responses showed a subtle appreciation of the initial gloomy presentation of the house in Coming Home: ‘darkness’/ ‘unlit’ even deathly; ‘drear’/’shrouded’ and how this changed and became a place at first of contentment as the home ‘revives’/ ‘relaxes’ and then came alive ‘pulse’/ ‘breathes’. At the lower end, weaker responses took a more literal approach to the end of the poem and commented that there were snakes in the garden.

The comparisons were often thoughtful and perceptive with differences in perspective and mood competently discussed. The writers’ effective tone, and presentation of the warmth and coldness of the homes were sensitively explored. Candidates engaged on a personal level with the reflections of home presented in both poems. Many candidates made simple, descriptive often unhelpful comments about the structure or rhyme schemes of the poems which should be discouraged e.g., “both poems have an ABAB rhyme scheme”.

31 Candidates who had a clear understanding of both poems were able to present sensible, justifiable interpretations and readings of both poems. Nevertheless, most candidates made thoughtful links and contrasts between the poems and were engaged by their content. Finally, many commented on the poem’s apparent messages e.g., the difference between a house and a “home”; the positive and negative impact of home environment on people; the lasting impact that different experiences of “home” can have. The most sensitive responses made the link between the comforting nature of the resurrected version of home in Coming Home and the idiomatic nature of what a home “ought” to be in Home. Sensitive candidates also discussed the difference in power between the two poems: honing in on the “godlike” reference in Coming Home and the ability to make changes to the home, compared to the lack of power and "fake” negativity in Home. Overall, candidates gave every impression of having enjoyed writing about the poems and levels of engagement were very high.

Summary of Key Points

Characteristics of good poetry responses: • a thorough examination of the first poem in 3.1 • a thorough examination of the second poem in 3.2, either as a discrete element or as part of the comparison • clear comparison of ideas, mood and some reference to how the poets use language • detailed selection and coverage from each poem • comments exploring the meaning of these selections • spend about an hour on the poetry questions.

Ways in which performance can be improved: • ensure that the first poem is adequately analysed in 3.1 • ensure that the second poem is adequately analysed in depth in 3.2 • discuss a range of quotations to ensure coverage of the texts • practice commenting on a range of poems and poetic techniques, including imagery and figurative language • avoid spotting and labelling techniques and patterns with no reference to meaning • develop the use of supporting references to support understanding of subtext • avoid ‘over reading’ of hidden meanings in the poems • experience in reading poems where similar topics are handled differently by poets • rehearse timings across the exam to ensure sufficient time is given to the poetry • handwriting must be legible.
